answer:
Regulatory determination — EU MDR, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2023/607

1. Last date for placing on the market or putting into service

31 December 2028 (inclusive).

Legal basis: Article 120(3a)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR), as inserted by Article 1(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2023/607. For class IIa devices with a certificate issued under Directive 93/42/EEC that is valid by virtue of Article 120(2) MDR, the transitional date is 31 December 2028, provided the cumulative conditions of Article 120(3c) are met. The pre-2023 MDR date of 26 May 2024 is not the final class IIa date after Regulation (EU) 2023/607.

2. The two notified-body milestones

Both are conditions in Article 120(3c)(e) MDR and both must be satisfied:

(a) Formal application — no later than 26 May 2024.
The manufacturer, or an authorised representative, must have lodged a formal application with a notified body in accordance with Section 4.3, first subparagraph, of Annex VII MDR for conformity assessment in respect of the device covered by Article 120(3a) or 120(3b), or a device intended to substitute it.

(b) Written agreement — no later than 26 September 2024.
The notified body and the manufacturer must have signed a written agreement in accordance with Section 4.3, second subparagraph, of Annex VII MDR for the conformity assessment of that device or a substitute device.

Summary table

| Item | Date | Legal provision |
|---|---|---|
| Last date to place on the market / put into service under the legacy transition | 31 December 2028 | MDR Art. 120(3a)(b), as amended by Reg. (EU) 2023/607 |
| Formal application lodged with a notified body | 26 May 2024 | MDR Art. 120(3c)(e), first limb |
| Written agreement signed with the notified body | 26 September 2024 | MDR Art. 120(3c)(e), second limb |

3. Conditions and effect of failure

Article 120(3c) is cumulative. In addition to the two notified-body milestones, the device must continue to comply with Directive 93/42/EEC, there must be no significant changes in design and intended purpose, the device must not present an unacceptable risk, and the manufacturer must have put in place a quality management system in accordance with Article 10(9) MDR no later than 26 May 2024. If any Article 120(3c) condition is not met, the 31 December 2028 extension in Article 120(3a) is not available; the device would then need to be placed on the market under another available route, ordinarily MDR certification.

4. Placement versus sell-off

The 31 December 2028 date is the last date for new placing on the market or putting into service under the Article 120(3a) transitional route. It is not a distributor sell-by date. Under Article 120(4) MDR, devices lawfully placed on the market under Article 120(3a) may continue to be made available on the market or put into service after that date without a sell-off deadline. This means devices already placed on the market by 31 December 2028 can remain in the supply chain and can still be put into service thereafter; the restriction is on new placement/putting into service under the legacy transition.

5. Scope notes

This is the EU/EEA MDR position. Switzerland and Northern Ireland have separate implementing arrangements and should be checked if those markets are relevant. There is no separate software, wireless or remote tier in Article 120(3a); a class IIa device remains in the 31 December 2028 tier. The final enacted text uses Article 120(3c); the Commission proposal had the conditions in Article 120(3d), which was renumbered in the adopted regulation.

question: X5
answer:
SCOPE DETERMINATION — EU LOW VOLTAGE DIRECTIVE (LVD) 2014/35/EU

=====================================================================
1. THE INSTRUMENT AND ITS OPERATIVE SCOPE TEXT
=====================================================================

The 'EU harmonisation law on the safety of electrical equipment within certain voltage limits' is Directive 2014/35/EU of 26 February 2014 (recast), OJ L 96, 29.3.2014, pp. 357-374, applicable since 20 April 2016.

Article 1, second paragraph, verbatim:

  'This Directive shall apply to electrical equipment designed for use with a
   voltage rating of between 50 and 1 000 V for alternating current and
   between 75 and 1 500 V for direct current, other than the equipment and
   phenomena listed in Annex II.'

=====================================================================
2. ANSWER TO ASK 1 — THE SCOPE VOLTAGE BANDS
=====================================================================

  Alternating current (AC):  50 V  to  1 000 V
  Direct current (DC):       75 V  to  1 500 V

Both bands are rated-voltage bands, not operating-window bands. A product is brought into scope when its voltage rating falls in either band. Points of construction that follow from the text and from the Commission's published guidance:

(a) RATED, NOT OPERATING. The figure compared against the bands is the rated input voltage or the rated output voltage of the equipment, not voltages that appear inside it. The Commission's guidance is explicit: 'Voltage ratings refer to the voltage of the electrical input or output, not to voltages which may appear inside the equipment ... Internally there may be higher voltages.'

(b) EITHER END COUNTS. Equipment is in scope if EITHER its rated input voltage OR its rated output voltage lies inside the band. A unit with a 230 V AC input and a 24 V AC output is therefore in scope on its input rating, even though its output is far below 50 V.

(c) ANY ONE RATING IS ENOUGH. If a product carries several ratings (multi-tap transformer, 115/230 V selector, 24 V AC and 400 V AC variants under one model family), the equipment is in scope if any one of its rated voltages falls inside the band.

(d) AC RATINGS ARE RMS. Nameplate AC voltages are RMS values. (A '24 V AC' secondary has a peak of about 34 V; this does not move it, because the comparison is made on the RMS rating.)

(e) DC RATINGS are the DC value stated on the rating plate.

(f) BOUNDARY VALUES. The Directive says 'between'. Market-surveillance and Commission practice reads the limits as inclusive: equipment rated exactly 50 V AC, 1 000 V AC, 75 V DC or 1 500 V DC is treated as in scope. This is the conservative reading and the one to design and document against. A product rated 49 V AC is out; one rated 50 V AC is in.

(g) THREE-PHASE. For three-phase equipment the rated voltage is taken as the line-to-line (phase-to-phase) voltage — i.e. 400 V for a 230/400 V three-phase machine. (Verify-item: this convention is guidance-level practice, not text in the Article 1 passage quoted above; it does not affect either ask.)

(h) ANNEX II EXCLUSIONS OVERRIDE THE VOLTAGE TEST. Equipment that is inside the bands but is one of the categories listed in Annex II is still out of scope. The categories (verify against the Annex II text in the consolidated version before relying on any of them in a technical file): explosive atmospheres; radiology and medical purposes; electrical parts of goods and passenger lifts; electricity meters; plugs and socket outlets for domestic use; electric fence controllers; radio-electrical interference; specialised equipment for ships, aircraft or railways complying with international safety provisions; custom-built evaluation kits for professional R&D use. The Annex II list was not in the fetched passages, so treat the wording as a prompt to open Annex II, not as a quotation.

=====================================================================
3. ANSWER TO ASK 2 — IS 24 V AC EQUIPMENT IN SCOPE?
=====================================================================

VERDICT: NO — not on the strength of a 24 V AC rating.

  24 V AC  <  50 V AC  (lower bound of the AC band)

24 V AC sits 26 V below the lower AC limit and 51 V below the lower DC limit. A product whose only external electrical rating is 24 V AC is outside the scope of Directive 2014/35/EU and must not be CE marked under it.

The verdict holds ONLY if all four of the following are true. Each is a real configuration that reverses the answer:

  (i)   No integrated power supply. If the 24 V AC is generated inside the enclosure from a mains supply — e.g. a 230 V AC / 24 V AC transformer or a 230 V AC input switch-mode PSU on the same PCB or in the same housing — then the equipment's rated INPUT voltage is 230 V AC, which is inside 50-1000 V AC, and the whole unit is in scope. The Commission guidance is direct on this: 'equipment with integrated power supply unit within the voltage ranges of the Directive, are in the scope of the LVD.'

  (ii)  No mains adaptor or transformer in the box. If the product is sold with an external 230 V AC / 24 V AC transformer or adaptor that is required for it to operate, that accessory is itself in scope and needs its own LVD conformity. Where the accessory is part of the single product placed on the market, the combination is in scope on its 230 V AC input rating. Where the adaptor is a separately CE-marked item placed on the market by another manufacturer, the 24 V AC equipment stays out of LVD scope but the adaptor's EU Declaration of Conformity must be held in the technical file.

  (iii) No other rating in band. A unit with a 24 V AC control input but a 230 V AC or 400 V AC power input is in scope. So is a unit with a 24 V AC input and a 24 V DC output? No — 24 V DC is below 75 V DC, so that one stays out. But a unit with a 24 V AC input and a 110 V DC output is in scope on its output rating.

  (iv)  Not excluded-and-not-caught elsewhere. Confirm no Annex II exclusion applies and no other instrument imposes its own voltage-independent regime (see section 5).

Internally generated high voltage does NOT bring a 24 V AC product into scope: a 24 V AC luminaire, sensor or actuator that internally produces a high ignition or inverter voltage remains outside LVD scope on the input/output test. Its safety is still a legal obligation — just under a different instrument (section 5).

=====================================================================
4. DECISION PROCEDURE (apply to any product)
=====================================================================

Step 1  Enumerate every external electrical input and output of the product AS PLACED ON THE MARKET, including any accessory supplied in the box that is required for use.
Step 2  For each, record the RATED voltage from the rating plate / technical file (RMS for AC, DC value for DC). Do not use measured operating voltages or internal rail voltages.
Step 3  Compare each rating against its own band:
          AC in 50-1000 V?  -> in scope
          DC in 75-1500 V?  -> in scope
        Any single 'yes' puts the equipment in scope.
Step 4  If in scope: check Annex II exclusions. If none applies, the full LVD regime runs — Annex I safety objectives, harmonised standards (e.g. EN IEC 62368-1, EN 60335 series, EN 61558 for transformers), technical file, EU Declaration of Conformity, CE marking.
Step 5  If out of scope on every rating: record the determination and its arithmetic in the technical file (e.g. 'sole external rating 24 V AC RMS; below the 50 V AC lower limit of Art. 1 of 2014/35/EU; LVD not applicable'), and apply the instruments in section 5 instead.

=====================================================================
5. WHAT APPLIES WHEN THE PRODUCT IS OUT OF LVD SCOPE
=====================================================================

Being outside the LVD is not being outside EU product law. For a 24 V AC product placed on the EU market, the usual stack is:

  - General Product Safety Regulation (EU) 2023/988, applicable since 13 December 2024, which repealed and replaced the General Product Safety Directive 2001/95/EC. This is the safety backstop for consumer products below the LVD thresholds. (Note: the Commission LVD page quoted in the source material still cites GPSD 2001/95/EC; that citation is now superseded.)
  - EMC Directive 2014/30/EU — applies on its own terms, with no voltage threshold.
  - RoHS 2011/65/EU and WEEE 2012/19/EU.
  - Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU if the product has any radio function (and note RED Article 3(1)(a) then supplies the safety requirement itself).
  - Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC (Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 applies from 20 January 2027) if the product is machinery; a 24 V AC control component may be a partly-completed machine, which carries its own documentation duties.
  - Battery Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 if applicable.

=====================================================================
6. WORKED CASES
=====================================================================

  Case A  24 V AC solenoid valve, no PSU, no other rating.
           -> OUT of LVD scope (24 < 50). GPSR + EMC + RoHS.

  Case B  Same valve with a 230 V AC/24 V AC transformer inside the same housing.
           -> IN scope. Rated input 230 V AC is in 50-1000 V AC. Whole unit CE marked under LVD.

  Case C  24 V AC device shipped with a separate CE-marked 230 V AC adaptor.
           -> Device OUT of LVD scope; adaptor IN scope and separately CE marked. Hold the adaptor DoC.

  Case D  24 V AC input, 24 V DC output controller.
           -> OUT of LVD scope (24 < 50 AC; 24 < 75 DC).

  Case E  24 V AC input, 110 V DC output drive.
           -> IN scope on the output rating (110 V DC is in 75-1500 V DC).

  Case F  48 V AC product.
           -> OUT of LVD scope (48 < 50). This is the near-miss case most often got wrong; check it against the inclusive boundary reading.

  Case G  50 V AC product.
           -> IN scope (boundary inclusive). Design and document as in scope.

=====================================================================
7. NOTES FOR THE HARDWARE FILE
=====================================================================

  - Put the voltage-scope determination in the technical file as a one-line calculation with the Article 1 limits quoted, whichever way it goes. This is the single document that settles a market-surveillance question at the border.
  - The rating plate is the evidence. If the plate says '24 V AC' but the BOM shows an on-board 230 V AC PSU, the plate is wrong and the product is in scope — fix the plate, not the determination.
  - Keep the boundary cases (48-52 V AC, 70-80 V DC) on a watch list; a variant change that nudges a rating across a limit changes the conformity route.
  - For Great Britain, the parallel instrument is the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016, which carries the same 50-1000 V AC / 75-1500 V DC limits, so the same determination holds; Northern Ireland remains under 2014/35/EU via the Windsor Framework.

=====================================================================
8. VERIFY-ITEMS (not sourced from the fetched passages; do not quote as text)
=====================================================================

  - The full Annex II exclusion list in section 2(h): open the consolidated Annex II before citing any category.
  - The three-phase line-to-line convention in section 2(g): guidance-level practice.
  - The inclusive treatment of the exact boundary values in section 2(f): practice-based; the Directive says only 'between'. The conservative reading is stated and is what the worked cases use.

question: X8
answer:
# MEMORANDUM — Article 14 CRA reporting obligation arising on 17 November 2026

## 1. Question presented

A manufacturer placed a connected consumer product on the EU market in 2025. On 17 November 2026 it becomes aware that a vulnerability in that product is being actively exploited. Does the EU Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, "CRA") oblige it to report now, and what are the deadlines for (a) the early warning, (b) the vulnerability notification and (c) the final report?

## 2. Answer in short

**Yes. The obligation is live and the clock is already running.** Reporting under Article 14 CRA has applied since **11 September 2026**, and it applies to every in-scope product with digital elements made available on the Union market — **including products placed on the market before 11 December 2027**, and including products whose support period has already ended. A 2025 placement therefore gives the manufacturer no temporal defence.

| # | Filing | Runs from | Deadline | Anchor date for awareness on 17 Nov 2026 |
|---|--------|-----------|----------|------------------------------------------|
| 2 | Early warning notification | moment of awareness | without undue delay, and in any event **within 24 hours** | **18 November 2026** |
| 3 | Vulnerability notification ("main" notification) | moment of awareness | without undue delay, and in any event **within 72 hours** | **20 November 2026** |
| 4 | Final report | **the moment a corrective or mitigating measure becomes available** (not the moment of awareness) | no later than **14 days** after that measure is available | fix date + 14 days (e.g. patch released 1 Dec 2026 → report by 15 Dec 2026) |

The 24 h and 72 h limits are outer limits only; "without undue delay" means a manufacturer that can file sooner must file sooner. The deadlines run in **clock hours/days, not working days** — no weekend or holiday extension applies.

## 3. Legal basis

- **Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (CRA)**, in force 10 December 2024.
- **Article 14 CRA** — reporting obligations of manufacturers (cited in the Commission's own guidance as "Article 14(1) and (3)").
- **Article 69(3) and Article 71(2), second sentence, CRA** — Article 14 applies from 11 September 2026.
- **Commission guidance C/2026/6013** on the application of Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, OJ C series, 17.11.2026, paras 209–210 (interpretive, non-binding, but the clearest statement of the temporal scope).
- **Article 3 CRA** — definitions of "product with digital elements", "actively exploited vulnerability", "severe incident".
- **Article 13 and Annex I, Part II CRA** — vulnerability handling obligations (separate from, and additional to, reporting).

## 4. Analysis

### 4.1 Scope — is there an obligation at all?

A connected consumer product is a **product with digital elements** (hardware or software connected directly or indirectly to a device or network) made available on the Union market. The CRA applies to manufacturers placing such products on the EU market **regardless of whether the manufacturer is established in the Union**; a non-EU manufacturer must designate an authorised representative in the Union by written mandate, but the reporting duty itself stays with the manufacturer.

The only scope exit relevant here is the **sector-specific exclusion**: products covered by the Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/745, the IVD Regulation (EU) 2017/746, vehicle type-approval Regulation (EU) 2019/2144, civil aviation Regulation (EU) 2018/1139, or marine equipment Directive (EU) 2014/90 fall outside the CRA (and are governed by their own incident-reporting regimes). A general consumer connected product is not in any of those categories. Free and open-source software is only in scope where it is placed on the market as part of a commercial activity; that is not the case described.

**Conclusion:** on the facts given, the product is in scope.

### 4.2 Temporal application — why 2025 placement is irrelevant

Commission guidance C/2026/6013, para 210, is explicit: under Article 69(3) and Article 71(2), second sentence, **the Article 14 obligation applies from 11 September 2026 to all products with digital elements within the scope of the CRA, including products placed on the market before 11 December 2027.** It further states that, unlike the vulnerability-handling obligations (which run only for the support period), **the reporting obligations continue to apply after a product is no longer supported.** The manufacturer of a product placed in 2025 whose support period has ended still owes the Article 14 notifications; it simply does not owe the Annex I Part II vulnerability-handling obligations.

17 November 2026 is after 11 September 2026. The reporting regime is in force.

### 4.3 The trigger and the moment of awareness

Article 14(1) is triggered by the manufacturer **becoming aware** of an **actively exploited vulnerability** contained in its product with digital elements. An actively exploited vulnerability is one for which there is reliable evidence that a malicious actor has exploited it in an information system without the permission of the system's owner or user. The facts state that exploitation is occurring and that the manufacturer has become aware on 17 November 2026, so the trigger is met.

**Practical point that decides whether the filing is late:** the clock runs from the moment the manufacturer *became aware*, not from the moment it finished its analysis, not from the moment it notified customers, and not from the moment a fix exists. If internal awareness in fact pre-dated 17 November 2026 (e.g. a threat-intelligence hit or a customer report received earlier but not escalated), the deadlines move earlier and the 17 November date is already a late start. The manufacturer should fix the T0 timestamp in writing immediately (who knew what, when, and on what evidence) and preserve that record.

### 4.4 Who must be notified, and how

Notification is made **simultaneously to (i) the CSIRT designated as coordinator for the Member State in which the manufacturer has its main establishment and (ii) ENISA**. Submission is through ENISA's **single reporting platform (SRP)**, which is the single entry point and routes the information to the coordinator CSIRT, other relevant CSIRTs, ENISA and, where necessary, the competent market surveillance authorities. A manufacturer with no Union main establishment files through the SRP on the same basis; the authorised representative does not displace the manufacturer's duty.

Importers and distributors do not carry the Article 14 duty in the ordinary case, but must pass information to the manufacturer, and an importer or distributor that places the product on the market under its own name or trade mark, or that carries out a substantial modification, is treated as the manufacturer and inherits the reporting duty.

### 4.5 Content of each filing

- **Early warning (≤24 h):** notification that an actively exploited vulnerability is suspected, indicating, where applicable, the Member States on whose territory the product has been made available, and any corrective or mitigating measures already taken. It is a short, factual alert — it is not the full technical analysis, and the absence of a fix is not a reason to delay it.
- **Vulnerability notification (≤72 h):** general information about the vulnerability, its severity and impact, and, where available, indicators of compromise.
- **Final report (≤14 days after the remedy is available):** description of the vulnerability, its severity and impact, the corrective or mitigating measures taken, and — where appropriate — the date the security update or workaround was made available.

### 4.6 The final-report deadline — read the anchor carefully

For an actively exploited vulnerability the final report is **not** due 14 days after awareness. It is due **no later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure becomes available**. Two consequences follow:

1. If a patch or workaround already existed at the moment of awareness, the 14 days run from that moment and the final report is due on or before 31 November — i.e. **1 December 2026**.
2. If no remedy exists yet, the 14-day period has not started, but the manufacturer must keep the CSIRT/ENISA informed and must not treat the silence as the end of the matter. The final report falls due 14 days after the remedy lands (patch on 1 December 2026 → final report by 15 December 2026).

### 4.7 Parallel severe-incident track

If the exploitation also amounts to a **severe incident having an impact on the security of the product**, a second chain runs in parallel: early warning within 24 hours, incident notification within 72 hours, and a **final report within one month of the 72-hour notification**. The same SRP submission can carry both, but the two final reports have different anchors and different deadlines and must not be conflated. This memo answers ask 4 on the vulnerability track (14 days); the incident track is a separate, additional deliverable if the severity threshold is met.

### 4.8 Ancillary obligations that attach on the same facts

- Notify the person or entity maintaining any integrated component (including an open-source component) in which the vulnerability sits, and remediate it in the product.
- Make a security update available to users free of charge and inform users about the vulnerability and the corrective measures.
- Maintain the coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy and the single point of contact for user reports.

### 4.9 Consequences of late or missing filing

Member States must lay down penalties for infringement; the CRA sets tiers of administrative fines, with the highest tier reserved for breaches of the essential cybersecurity requirements. **Microenterprises and small enterprises cannot be fined for failure to meet the 24-hour deadline** for reporting vulnerabilities and severe incidents — but the obligation itself is unchanged and the filing is still due.

## 5. Worked timeline (awareness = Tuesday 17 November 2026, time T0)

| Time | Event | Action |
|------|-------|--------|
| T0, Tue 17 Nov 2026 | Awareness of active exploitation | Fix and record T0; open SRP draft; escalate to the security lead |
| T0 + 24 h → **Wed 18 Nov 2026** | Early warning deadline | Submit early warning via SRP to coordinator CSIRT + ENISA; list Member States of availability and measures taken |
| T0 + 72 h → **Fri 20 Nov 2026** | Vulnerability notification deadline | Submit vulnerability notification with severity, impact, IoCs where available |
| Remedy date + 14 d | Final report deadline | Submit final report (e.g. remedy 1 Dec 2026 → **15 Dec 2026**) |
| If severe incident: 72 h notification + 1 month | Incident final report | Separate filing, separate deadline |

All dates are calendar-based; the 72-hour deadline falls on a Friday, so no weekend question arises, and in any event the CRA does not extend deadlines for weekends or public holidays.

## 6. What would change this answer

- **Excluded sector.** If the product is a medical device, IVD, type-approved vehicle, civil aviation or marine equipment product, the CRA does not apply and the answer must be re-run against that sector's own incident-reporting regime.
- **Earlier awareness.** If internal awareness pre-dated 17 November 2026, the 24 h and 72 h deadlines have already expired and the exposure is a late-filing one, not a planning one.
- **Not "actively exploited".** Without reliable evidence of exploitation the Article 14 chain is not triggered; the Article 13 vulnerability-handling and Annex I Part II obligations still apply.
- **Small-enterprise status.** Changes the fining exposure for the 24-hour deadline only, not the deadline.
- **Non-EU establishment.** Authorised-representative requirement applies; the reporting duty does not move.

## 7. Sources relied on

- Commission guidance on the application of Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, OJ C/2026/6013, 17.11.2026, paras 209–210 (Article 14 duty; application from 11 September 2026 to all in-scope products including those placed before 11 December 2027; reporting survives end of support).
- European Commission, Cyber Resilience Act summary (24 h early warning; 72 h main notification; final report ≤14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available; final report ≤1 month for severe incidents; Article 14 applies from 11 September 2026).
- Belgian Centre for Cybersecurity (CCB), CRA page (reporting via the Single Reporting Platform from 11 September 2026; 24 h / 72 h / 14 days / 1 month chain).
- BSI, Cyber Resilience Act page (24 h / 72 h / 14 days / 1 month; excluded sectors; CRA applies to manufacturers regardless of establishment).
- European Parliament Legislative Observatory summary of the CRA (Article 14 reporting obligations of manufacturers).

question: X11
shape: UN vehicle regulation (electric power train, UN R100)
answer:
Governing clause: UN Regulation No. 100, 05 series (OJ L, 2026/1695), paragraph 5.1.3.2, 'Electric power train consisting of combined DC- and AC-buses'. Because the 400 V AC and DC buses are galvanically connected, the combined-bus rule applies rather than the separate-bus values of 5.1.3.1.

Default combined-bus requirement, with no AC protection measures:
  minimum isolation resistance = 500 ohm/V of working voltage U
  U = 400 V
  R_min = 500 ohm/V x 400 V = 200,000 ohm = 200 kΩ

Exception when all AC high-voltage buses are protected by one of the two measures listed in 5.1.3.2:
  minimum isolation resistance = 100 ohm/V of working voltage U
  R_min = 100 ohm/V x 400 V = 40,000 ohm = 40 kΩ

The two measures in 5.1.3.2 are:
  (a) at least two or more layers of solid insulators, electrical protection barriers or enclosures that meet the requirement in paragraph 5.1.1 independently, for example a wiring harness;
  (b) mechanically robust protections that have sufficient durability over vehicle service life, such as motor housings, electronic converter cases or connectors.

Answers to the request:
  (a) AC buses with none of the extra protections: 200 kΩ minimum between the high-voltage bus and the electrical chassis.
  (b) All AC buses protected by one of the two measures: 40 kΩ minimum between the high-voltage bus and the electrical chassis.

Notes: No separate absolute kΩ minimum is stated in the quoted clause; the requirement is the ohm-per-volt criterion above. Paragraph 5.1.3.2 permits demonstration by calculation, measurement or a combination of both, with measurement conducted according to Annex 5A. The calculation assumes the given 400 V is the Regulation's working voltage and that the vehicle is within the 5.1.3.2 combined-bus case, i.e. not excluded by the opening sentence of 5.1.3.
cautions: The answer gives 200 kΩ for ask 1, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

# Regulatory determination — Bluetooth-connected insulin pump (MDR device) and the RED cybersecurity essential requirements

## A. Determination in brief

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| 1. Do the essential requirements of Article 3(3), points (d), (e) and (f), of Directive 2014/53/EU, as specified by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30, apply to a Bluetooth-connected insulin pump that is a medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745? | **No.** Article 2(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 disapplies all three points to radio equipment to which Regulation (EU) 2017/745 also applies. |
| 2. From what date does Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 apply to radio equipment that it does cover? | **1 August 2025** (ISO 2025-08-01), per Article 3 as amended by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2444. |

---

## B. Ask 1 — applicability to the pump

### B.1 The operative text

Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30, **Article 2(1)** (consolidated text 02022R0030-20231027):

> "By way of derogation from Article 1, the essential requirements set out in Article 3(3), points (d), (e) and (f), of Directive 2014/53/EU shall not apply to radio equipment to which either of the following Union legislation also applies:
> (a) Regulation (EU) 2017/745;
> (b) Regulation (EU) 2017/746."

Recital (15) of the same Regulation states the policy behind it:

> "Both Regulations (EU) 2017/745 and (EU) 2017/746 address certain elements of cybersecurity risks associated with the risks addressed by Article 3(3), points (d), (e) and (f), of Directive 2014/53/EU. Radio equipment to which either of those Regulations apply should therefore not fall within the categories or classes of radio equipment which should comply with the essential requirements set out in Article 3(3), points (d), (e) and (f), of Directive 2014/53/EU."

### B.2 The test sequence, applied

| # | Test | Result for this pump | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Is the product radio equipment within the RED (does it intentionally emit/ receive radio waves for radiocommunication or radiodetermination)? | **Yes** — Bluetooth is a radio interface; the pump is radio equipment. (If Bluetooth is delivered by an integrated module, the pump as placed on the market is still the radio equipment; see B.4.) | RED 2014/53/EU; project assumption, to be confirmed against the bill of materials |
| 2 | Does the product fall within a category/class described in Article 1 of DR 2022/30? | **Probably yes for (d) and (e), no for (f).** Art 1(1) catches any radio equipment that "can communicate itself over the internet, whether it communicates directly or via any other equipment" — a pump that syncs via a companion smartphone app or a home hub meets this. Art 1(2) additionally catches "radio equipment designed or intended, whether exclusively or not exclusively, to be worn on, strapped to, or hung from any part of the human body" — a patch/infusion-set pump meets this, and Art 1(2)(a) catches internet-connected equipment capable of processing personal data (glucose/insulin data are personal data). Art 1(3)/(f) applies only where the equipment "enables the holder or user to transfer money, monetary value or virtual currency" — an insulin pump does not. | DR 2022/30 Art 1(1), 1(2)(a) and (d), 1(3) |
| 3 | Does any Union legislation listed in Article 2(1) also apply to that radio equipment? | **Yes — Regulation (EU) 2017/745 applies**, because the pump is a medical device under the MDR. | Stated premise of the question |

AES-256 parameters per FIPS 197 (FIPS PUB 197, 26 November 2001; updated 9 May 2023 with no technical changes to the algorithm).

ANSWERS
1. Rounds: 14 (Nr = 14).
2. Block size: 128 bits (Nb = 4 words).
3. Round keys consumed: 15 (Nr + 1), each an array of four 32-bit words (128 bits); 15 × 4 = 60 words total, i.e. 4(Nr+1) = 4·15 = 60 words = 1920 bits of expanded key schedule.

DERIVATION AND CITATIONS

Ask 1 — Number of rounds.
FIPS 197 §6.3 states: 'For the AES algorithm, the number of rounds to be performed during the execution of the algorithm is dependent on the key size. The number of rounds is represented by Nr, where Nr = 10 when Nk = 4, Nr = 12 when Nk = 6, and Nr = 14 when Nk = 8.' AES-256 has a 256-bit cipher key, and §6.3 defines Nk as the number of 32-bit words in the Cipher Key: Nk = 256/32 = 8. Hence Nr = 14. Figure 4 ('Key-Block-Round Combinations') tabulates it explicitly:

  Key Length (Nk words) | Block Size (Nb words) | Number of Rounds (Nr)
  AES-128: 4            | 4                     | 10
  AES-192: 6            | 4                     | 12
  AES-256: 8            | 4                     | 14

Ask 2 — Block size in bits.
FIPS 197 §3.1: 'The input and output for the AES algorithm each consist of sequences of 128 bits... The sequences will sometimes be referred to as blocks.' §6.3: 'For the AES algorithm, the length of the input block, the output block and the State is 128 bits. This is represented by Nb = 4, which reflects the number of 32-bit words (number of columns) in the State.' Unit conversion check: Nb = 4 words × 32 bits/word = 128 bits. The block size is fixed at 128 bits for all three variants (AES-128, AES-192, AES-256); only the key length and round count vary.

Ask 3 — Number of round keys, each an array of four words.
FIPS 197 §5.2 (Key Expansion): 'The key expansion routine... generates a total of Nb(Nr + 1) words.' For AES-256: Nb = 4, Nr = 14, so 4 × (14 + 1) = 60 words. Each round key is one column-array of Nb = 4 words = 128 bits, so the number of round keys is 60 / 4 = 15 = Nr + 1.

Why 15 and not 14: the cipher applies AddRoundKey 15 times, not 14. FIPS 197 §5.1 (Cipher) pseudocode:

  Cipher(byte in[4*Nb], byte out[4*Nb], word w[Nb*(Nr+1)])
    state = in
    AddRoundKey(state, w[0, Nb-1])              // round key 0 — initial whitening, before round 1
    for round = 1 step 1 to Nr-1:
        SubBytes(state); ShiftRows(state); MixColumns(state)
        AddRoundKey(state, w[round*Nb, (round+1)*Nb-1])
    SubBytes(state); ShiftRows(state)            // final round, no MixColumns
    AddRoundKey(state, w[Nr*Nb, (Nr+1)*Nb-1])    // round key Nr
    out = state

That is one AddRoundKey before the loop plus one per round for rounds 1..14 = 1 + 14 = 15 key additions, indexed w[0..3], w[4..7], ..., w[56..59]. So the cipher consumes exactly Nr + 1 = 15 round keys of four words each.

KEY SCHEDULE DETAIL FOR AES-256 (for implementers)
Nk = 8, Nb = 4, Nr = 14. Total words to generate: Nb(Nr+1) = 60.
- w[0..7] are copied verbatim from the 256-bit cipher key (8 words = 256 bits).
- w[8..59] (52 words) are generated by the expansion loop.
- For i from Nk to Nb(Nr+1)-1:
    temp = w[i-1]
    if i mod Nk == 0:      temp = SubWord(RotWord(temp)) xor Rcon[i/Nk]
    else if Nk > 6 and i mod Nk == 4:  temp = SubWord(temp)   // AES-256 only
    w[i] = w[i-Nk] xor temp
- The 'else if Nk > 6 and i mod Nk == 4' branch is specific to AES-256 (Nk = 8): an extra SubWord is applied every eighth word, at i ≡ 4 (mod 8). This is the only structural difference in the key schedule versus AES-128/192.
- Rcon values used for AES-256: Rcon[1..7] = 01, 02, 04, 08, 10, 20, 40 (i/Nk ranges 1..7 since i runs 8..59 in steps of 8 for the RotWord branch).

Grouping the 60 words into round keys (each an array of four words, little-endian byte order within a word per §3.3/§5.2 conventions):
  Round key  0: w[0],  w[1],  w[2],  w[3]    (initial AddRoundKey)
  Round key  1: w[4],  w[5],  w[6],  w[7]
  ...
  Round key 14: w[56], w[57], w[58], w[59]   (final round)
  => 15 round keys, indices 0 through Nr = 14.

ARITHMETIC CROSS-CHECKS (all consistent)
- Round keys = Nr + 1 = 14 + 1 = 15.
- Words = 4(Nr + 1) = 4 × 15 = 60; and 15 round keys × 4 words = 60 words.
- Bits of key schedule = 60 words × 32 bits = 1920 bits; and 15 round keys × 128 bits = 1920 bits.
- Round-key width = Nb words = 4 words = 128 bits = block size. Round keys are the same width as the State.
- Generated (non-verbatim) words = 60 − Nk = 60 − 8 = 52.
- Comparison table, to confirm no cross-variant confusion:
    AES-128: Nk=4, Nb=4, Nr=10, round keys 11, expanded words 44
    AES-192: Nk=6, Nb=4, Nr=12, round keys 13, expanded words 52
    AES-256: Nk=8, Nb=4, Nr=14, round keys 15, expanded words 60
- Cipher-key bits vs. schedule bits: 256 input bits expand to 1920 bits (7.5×), which is expected since each of the 15 AddRoundKey steps needs a distinct 128-bit key.

SUMMARY OF FINAL VALUES
  AES-256 rounds (Nr) .............. 14
  AES-256 block size .............. 128 bits (Nb = 4 words)
  AES-256 round keys consumed ..... 15 (Nr + 1), each 4 words / 128 bits; 60 words / 1920 bits total

# NIST SP 800-171 — Security Requirement Family Counts and Rev. 2 Status

Documentation deliverable: a sourced findings memo answering three lookup questions. No repository, build, or execution context is involved; every figure below is a direct read of a NIST-published source, and the family lists are included so each count is self-verifying (a reader can recount from the list rather than take the number on trust).

## 1. Answers

| # | Question | Answer | Primary source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many families of security requirements does the **current** revision of SP 800-171 define? | **17 families** | NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3 (final, 14 May 2024); NIST Rev. 3 implementer briefing, which states: *"SP 800-171 security requirements are organized into 17 families"* |
| 2 | How many did **Revision 2** define? | **14 families** | NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 2 (February 2020), Section 3 structure |
| 3 | What is Revision 2's **status** on NIST's own published copy? | **Superseded** — published label: *"Superseded on May 14, 2024 by SP 800-171 Rev. 3"* | NIST CSRC publication record for SP 800-171 Rev. 2 (`csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/171/r2/upd1/final`) |

Current revision at answer time: **SP 800-171 Revision 3** (final). Earlier Rev. 3 drafts are not current — NIST marks the Rev. 3 Initial Public Draft as *"Obsoleted on November 09, 2023 by SP 800-171 Rev. 3 (Final Public Draft)"*, and the final publication superseded Rev. 2.

## 2. Ask 1 — Current revision (Rev. 3): 17 families

Rev. 3 restructured the requirement set against the SP 800-53 Rev. 5 / 800-53B moderate baseline. Its 17 families, in the publication's own order:

1. Access Control (AC)
2. Awareness and Training (AT)
3. Audit and Accountability (AU)
4. Configuration Management (CM)
5. Assessment, Authorization, and Monitoring (CA)
6. Contingency Planning (CP)
7. Identification and Authentication (IA)
8. Incident Response (IR)
9. Maintenance (MA)
10. Media Protection (MP)
11. Personnel Security (PS)
12. Physical and Environmental Protection (PE)
13. Risk Assessment (RA)
14. System and Services Acquisition (SA)
15. System and Communications Protection (SC)
16. System and Information Integrity (SI)
17. Supply Chain Risk Management (SR)

Count = 17.

## 3. Ask 2 — Revision 2: 14 families

Rev. 2's 14 families, in the publication's own order:

1. Access Control (AC)
2. Awareness and Training (AT)
3. Audit and Accountability (AU)
4. Configuration Management (CM)
5. Identification and Authentication (IA)
6. Incident Response (IR)
7. Maintenance (MA)
8. Media Protection (MP)
9. Personnel Security (PS)
10. Physical Protection (PE)
11. Risk Assessment (RA)
12. Security Assessment (CA)
13. System and Communications Protection (SC)
14. System and Information Integrity (SI)

Count = 14 (carrying the 110 security requirements Rev. 2 is known for).

**Delta check (14 → 17):** three families are added in Rev. 3 — Contingency Planning (CP), System and Services Acquisition (SA), Supply Chain Risk Management (SR). Two are renamed: Security Assessment (CA) → Assessment, Authorization, and Monitoring; Physical Protection (PE) → Physical and Environmental Protection. 14 + 3 = 17, consistent with Ask 1.

## 4. Ask 3 — Revision 2's status on NIST's copy

NIST's own publication record for SP 800-171 Rev. 2 carries the status designation **Superseded**, with the specific published wording *"Superseded on May 14, 2024 by SP 800-171 Rev. 3"* — i.e., NIST retained the Rev. 2 document (it is still downloadable from nvlpubs.nist.gov) but marked it as no longer the current version on the date Rev. 3 was published.

Terminology note, because NIST uses these labels distinctly and they are easy to conflate:

- **Superseded** — replaced by a newer revision of the same publication (Rev. 2's case).
- **Obsoleted** — a draft replaced by a later draft (the Rev. 3 Initial Public Draft's case).
- **Withdrawn** — pulled without a replacement.

Rev. 2 is *Superseded*, not Withdrawn and not Obsoleted. The Rev. 2 PDF itself is dated February 2020 and does not carry a supersession banner in every copy; the status designation is authoritative on the CSRC catalog page, not necessarily on the PDF cover.

## 5. Counting convention used (and the one it excludes)

"Families" here means **the numbered security-requirement family groupings the publication itself defines** (Access Control, Awareness and Training, …) — the sense in which NIST writes "organized into 17 families."

This is deliberately *not* the same axis as Rev. 2's **basic vs. derived** requirement categorization, which classifies individual requirements, not families, and does not change either family count. If a downstream consumer needs a basic/derived split or a total requirement count, that is a separate lookup against the publications' requirement tables and should not be substituted for the 17 / 14 figures above.

Also out of scope by design: SP 800-171A (assessment procedures), SP 800-172 / 800-172A (enhanced requirements), and SP 800-53 (control catalog). Their family structures are different publications and must not be conflated with SP 800-171's.

## 6. Re-verification procedure (NIST revises; re-check before reuse)

1. Open `csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/171/` and confirm which revision is listed as final/current. If a Rev. 4 (or a Rev. 3 update) is now current, **Ask 1's answer must be recomputed** from that publication's family structure — do not carry 17 forward by default.
2. Open the current revision's PDF at `nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-171r<N>.pdf`, go to the requirements section, and count the distinct family headings. Compare to the list in §2.
3. Open `csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/171/r2/upd1/final` and read the status line at the top of the record verbatim. If the wording has changed, quote the new wording; the expected form is "Superseded on May 14, 2024 by SP 800-171 Rev. 3."
4. Record the retrieval date alongside the three figures — status labels and "current revision" are time-dependent, the two family counts are not.

## 7. Confidence and limits

- **Ask 1 (17)** — high confidence; directly stated in NIST's Rev. 3 material and independently reproducible by counting the family headings in the Rev. 3 PDF (§2 list).
- **Ask 2 (14)** — high confidence; Rev. 2's 14-family / 110-requirement structure is stable and independently reproducible from the Rev. 2 PDF (§3 list).
- **Ask 3 (Superseded)** — high confidence on the designation itself. The retrieved excerpt set did not surface the status line character-for-character, so if exact quotation matters (e.g., for a compliance artifact), confirm the wording on the live CSRC record per §6 step 3. The substantive answer — Rev. 2 is superseded by Rev. 3, effective 14 May 2024 — is not in doubt.

# multiprocessing default start method on Linux — documented answer (CPython 3.15 series)

## Sources consulted (documentation text only, no interpreter inspection)

| ID | Page | Snapshot note |
|----|------|----------------|
| S1 | https://docs.python.org/3.15/library/multiprocessing.html | Primary. Current 3.15-series page; contains a `Changed in version 3.15.1` entry, so the snapshot is at least 3.15.1. |
| S2 | https://docs.python.org/3/library/multiprocessing.html | Redirect-to-current copy; identical wording to S1. |
| S3 | https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/multiprocessing.html | Cross-check; states the same POSIX carve-out as `3.14.9`. |
| S4 | python-docs `3.14` translation catalogue (`library/multiprocessing.po`) | Message-ids of the same English source text; used to confirm the `fork` / `forkserver` wording is source text, not translator paraphrase. |

A GitHub issue (lighteval #1400) independently says "forkserver became the default on Linux in Python 3.14"; it is used only as corroboration, never as the basis for an answer.

## Answers

### 1. Default on Linux in the 3.15 series when `set_start_method()` is never called

**`forkserver`** — in the ordinary case where the process has a writable temporary directory.

Documented basis (S1, S3):

> "Changed in version 3.14: On POSIX platforms the default start method was changed from *fork* to *forkserver* to retain the performance but avoid common multithreaded process incompatibilities. See gh-84559."

> "Changed in version 3.14: This became the default start method on POSIX platforms."  (attached to the *forkserver* entry)

> "Available on POSIX platforms which support passing file descriptors over Unix pipes such as Linux. The default on those."  (S4, message-id of the *forkserver* entry)

Linux is a POSIX platform that passes file descriptors over Unix pipes, so it is inside "those". There is no separate Linux-only paragraph and no glibc/musl distinction anywhere in the docs; the only documented carve-out for POSIX is the one in ask 3.

### 2. Linux default before Python 3.14

**`fork`**.

Documented basis (S1, S3, S4):

> "On POSIX platforms the default start method was changed from *fork* to *forkserver* …"

> "This is no longer the default start method on any platform. Code that requires *fork* must explicitly specify that via `get_context` or `set_start_method`."  (S4, *fork* entry)

"Changed from fork to forkserver" in 3.14 fixes the pre-3.14 value as `fork`; the second quote confirms `fork` is now the default nowhere, so it cannot have survived past 3.14 on Linux.

### 3. Condition under which the default becomes `spawn` instead

**When there is no writable temporary directory** — for example on a read-only file system.

Documented basis (S1):

> "Changed in version 3.15.1: *spawn* is now the default start method when there is no writable temporary directory, for example on a read-only file system. Previously *forkserver* remained the default there and starting a process failed with an `OSError`. The default is determined when it is first needed rather than when `multiprocessing` is imported. See gh-155717."

S3 states the identical change for the 3.14 line:

> "Changed in version 3.14.9: *spawn* is now the default start method when there is no writable temporary directory, for example on a read-only file system. …"

Three properties of this condition matter and are all documented above:

1. It is a **filesystem/environment** condition, not a Python-version condition. The version number only says *when the rule was introduced*.
2. It is evaluated **lazily** — "determined when it is first needed rather than when `multiprocessing` is imported". A program can therefore import `multiprocessing`, chdir, or remount `/tmp`, and the answer can differ from the import-time environment. (Mechanism, inference not quote: *forkserver* needs a Unix socket path in the temp dir, so an unwritable temp dir previously produced `OSError` at first process start — hence gh-155717.)
3. It **does not** apply to macOS or Windows, whose `spawn` default comes from a different, earlier rule (macOS since 3.8, bpo-33725; Windows historically).

## Consolidated version table (Linux only)

| Python version | Default on Linux, writable temp dir | Default on Linux, no writable temp dir |
|---|---|---|
| ≤ 3.13 | `fork` | `fork` |
| 3.14.0 – 3.14.8 | `forkserver` | `forkserver` (process start fails with `OSError`) |
| 3.14.9+ | `forkserver` | `spawn` |
| 3.15.0 | `forkserver` | `forkserver` (inferred: S1 attributes the change to 3.15.1, so 3.15.0 precedes it) |
| 3.15.1+ | `forkserver` | `spawn` |

The 3.15.0 row is the only inference in the table and is flagged as such; every other cell is a direct restatement of a quoted changelog entry.

## Caveats to attach to any reuse of these answers

- **Snapshot pinning.** S1 is the current 3.15-series page, not a frozen point release. Because it already carries a 3.15.1 entry, quoting it as "3.15.0 behaviour" would be wrong. Cite as "3.15 series, snapshot fetched 2026-11-18, sha256 0a06c38e4a4e".
- **Scope of "Linux".** The docs say "POSIX platforms"; Linux qualifies via the file-descriptor-over-Unix-pipes availability note. The docs draw no distinction between glibc and musl Linux, so none is claimed here.
- **`fork` is deprecated in practice on threaded processes.** From 3.14 onward, if CPython detects multiple threads, the internal `os.fork` raises `DeprecationWarning`. This is why the default moved off `fork` (gh-84559) and is the reason not to recommend `fork` as a workaround for code that no longer pickles under `forkserver`.
- **Setting the method still overrides everything.** `set_start_method('fork' | 'spawn' | 'forkserver', force=False)` raises `RuntimeError` if already set and `force` is not true; `set_start_method(None, force=False)` resets to the default context. Any answer above describes only the case where this is never called.
- **First use wins.** Per S1, `get_start_method(allow_none=False)`, `get_context(None)`, and even instantiating primitives such as `Lock`/`Semaphore`/`Event`/`Condition` "may set the global start method". A library that constructs a `multiprocessing.Lock` at import time can therefore freeze the default before user code runs.

## Verification procedure (for a human applying this)

1. Read the default without mutating it:
   `python -c "import multiprocessing as mp; print(mp.get_start_method(allow_none=True))"` — prints `None` when nothing has fixed the default yet.
2. Read the effective default (this *sets* it, as documented):
   `python -c "import multiprocessing as mp; print(mp.get_start_method())"`
3. Exercise the ask-3 condition without remounting anything: run step 2 with `TMPDIR` pointing at a non-writable directory (e.g. `TMPDIR=/proc python -c ...`, or a `chmod 500` temp dir) on 3.15.1+/3.14.9+ and compare with a writable `TMPDIR`. Expect `spawn` vs `forkserver`. On 3.14.0–3.14.8 and 3.15.0 expect `forkserver` followed by `OSError` at first process start.
4. Cross-check the changelog entry rather than the prose if the two ever disagree; the `Changed in version` blocks are the normative record of when the default moved.

## One-line answers

1. `forkserver` (3.15 series, Linux/POSIX, writable temp dir).
2. `fork` (all Linux/POSIX before 3.14).
3. `spawn` becomes the default only when there is no writable temporary directory (e.g. a read-only file system) — 3.15.1+ on the 3.15 line, 3.14.9+ on the 3.14 line.

# WebAssembly 3.0 core spec — linear memory limits

Scope: this answers the four asks as *specification* limits (what a module may declare and what `memory.grow` may reach under the core spec), not engine implementation limits. Engines are permitted by the spec's appendix on implementation limitations to impose smaller limits, and most do.

Source basis: WebAssembly Specification, Release 3.0 (the current draft line; the spec landing page fetched shows "Release 3.0 (2026-11-16)", and the memory64 landing page lists "WebAssembly 3.0 (Draft 2024)" — the memory64 proposal is merged into 3.0, which is why i64 address types appear in the 3.0 memory type). The four figures below come from the memory type / limits validation rules and the memory instance definition. I have not reproduced verbatim quotations because the fetched passages did not include those sections; the statements below are paraphrases of those rules, and the section pointers tell a reviewer exactly where to confirm each one.

## 1. Page size

**65536 bytes = 2^16 bytes = 64 KiB.**

Where it is fixed:
- *Structure → Memory*: a memory type is `limits addrtype`, and a memory instance's data is a byte vector whose length is the page count times the page size, with the page size defined as 2^16 bytes. This is the single constant that ties page counts to byte counts throughout the spec.
- *Execution → Memory Instructions* / *Memory Instances*: `memory.grow` adds pages by appending 2^16 bytes per page; `memory.size` returns the page count.

Do not conflate this with the host OS page size (commonly 4096 bytes on x86-64, 16384 on Apple silicon). The wasm page is 64 KiB regardless of host.

## 2. Maximum pages for an i32 address type

**65536 pages = 2^16 pages.**

Where it is fixed:
- *Validation → Types → Limits* (limits matching/validation): a limits pair `n .. m` is valid for address type `i32` iff `n <= m <= 2^16` (and, for a shared memory, `m` must be present). The same range constant is what `memory.grow` checks at runtime.

Important consequence: **the binary format is not the limit; validation is.** The limits are encoded as LEB128 unsigned integers (u32 for i32 memories), so the *encoding* can express values up to 2^32-1 — e.g. `0x80 0x80 0x04` (65536) is fine but a module declaring 131072 pages encodes without error and then **fails validation**. Any answer of the form "the binary format allows 2^32 pages" is wrong.

## 3. That maximum in bytes (i32)

**65536 pages × 65536 bytes/page = 4294967296 bytes = 2^32 bytes = 4 GiB.**

Consistency check: 2^32 bytes is exactly the addressable range of an unsigned 32-bit address (offsets 0 … 2^32−1). So the page bound and the byte bound coincide; a memory at the declared maximum is exactly addressable in full, with no wasted or unreachable tail. (This is why i32 addresses are interpreted as *unsigned* in effective-address computation — a signed interpretation would make the top half of a maximal memory unreachable.)

Unit note: 4294967296 bytes = 4 GiB (binary prefix) = 4.295 × 10^9 bytes. It is **not** "4 GB" in the SI sense. If you need one framing, use GiB.

## 4. Maximum pages for an i64 address type

**2^48 pages = 281474976710656 pages.**

Where it is fixed:
- *Validation → Types → Limits*: the limits range constant is `2^48` when the address type is `i64`. Limits are encoded as u64 LEB128 for i64 memories (limits flag bytes `0x04` = i64 with min only, `0x05` = i64 with min and max, in the binary format's memory/limits encoding), again with validation — not the encoding — enforcing the ceiling.

Byte equivalent, for completeness: 2^48 × 2^16 = **2^64 bytes = 18446744073709551616 bytes = 16 EiB**, i.e. exactly the addressable range of an unsigned 64-bit address. This resolves the plan's open question about "full 2^64-range maximum vs. 2^48 practical limit": **there is no divergence for i64.** The spec's declared page bound of 2^48 pages is precisely the count that spans a full 64-bit address space, so the declared bound and the address-space maximum are the same number expressed in different units.

## Summary table

| Ask | Quantity | Value | Unit | Power-of-two form |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Page size | 65536 | bytes | 2^16 B = 64 KiB |
| 2 | Max pages, addrtype i32 | 65536 | pages | 2^16 |
| 3 | Max bytes, addrtype i32 | 4294967296 | bytes | 2^32 B = 4 GiB |
| 4 | Max pages, addrtype i64 | 281474976710656 | pages | 2^48 ( = 2^64 B = 16 EiB ) |

## Applying this — worked examples

**Validate a declared maximum (i32).** For a memory declared `(memory 1 65536)`: min 1 ≤ max 65536 ≤ 2^16 → valid. `(memory 1 65537)` → invalid (`max` exceeds the i32 limits range). `(memory 65537)` (min only) → invalid, because min must also be ≤ 2^16.

**`memory.grow` semantics.** Growth fails (returns −1) if `current_pages + delta` exceeds the memory's declared `max`, or — absent a declared max — the address-type range constant (2^16 for i32, 2^48 for i64). So an i32 memory declared with min only can never exceed 65536 pages, and a request that would land exactly on 65536 pages succeeds.

**Byte arithmetic recipe.** bytes = pages × 65536; pages = bytes / 65536 (integer division; any remainder means the byte count is not page-aligned). 65536 pages → 4294967296 B; 281474976710656 pages → 18446744073709551616 B.

**Sanity invariants worth asserting in any test suite built on this:**
- `page_size == 1 << 16`
- `max_pages(addrtype) == 1 << (addr_bits - 16)` where `addr_bits ∈ {32, 64}`
- `max_bytes(addrtype) == 1 << addr_bits`
- `max_pages(i32) * page_size == 1 << 32` and `max_pages(i64) * page_size == 1 << 64`

## Pitfalls this answer deliberately avoids

- **Confusing spec limit with engine limit.** V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore, Wasmtime, WasmEdge and others cap far lower in practice (often ~4 GiB for i32 memories on 64-bit hosts, and a configurable, usually much smaller cap for memory64). "The spec says 4 GiB" is true; "my runtime will give me 4 GiB" is a separate, often false claim.
- **Answering the i64 limit as 2^32 pages** (the i32 number) or as 2^64 pages (which would be 2^80 bytes and exceeds the address space — arithmetically impossible for a 64-bit address). 2^48 is the only count consistent with 2^64 bytes.
- **Using the binary encoding's width as the limit.** u32/u64 LEB128 ranges are encoding ranges, not validation ranges.
- **Treating 4 GiB as 4 000 000 000 bytes.** The correct figure is 4294967296 bytes.
- **Conflating host page size with wasm page size.** The 65536-byte constant is spec-level and host-independent.

## Verification pointers (for a reviewer who wants verbatim text)

Read, in the WebAssembly 3.0 core spec at https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/ :
1. *Structure → Types → Memory Types* — the `limits addrtype` production.
2. *Validation → Types → Limits* — the rule giving the range constant 2^16 for `i32` and 2^48 for `i64`.
3. *Execution → Memory Instances* — the page size constant 2^16 bytes.
4. *Execution → Instructions → Memory Instructions* — `memory.grow` failure conditions.
5. *Binary Format → Types → Limits* — flag bytes `0x00/0x01/0x04/0x05` and LEB128 widths.
6. *Appendix → Implementation Limitations* — the spec's permission for engines to be stricter than these maxima.

Section titles are stable across 2.0 and 3.0; only the `addrtype` parameter and the i64 limits range are new in 3.0.

ANSWER — DOMESTIC MICROWAVE OVEN, SAME UNIT SHIPPED TO CANADA AND THE US

Measurement basis common to all three answers: leakage power density in mW/cm2 at points at least 5 cm from the oven's external surface, with the oven fully assembled and operating with service and user controls adjusted to yield maximum output.

| Ask | Jurisdiction / condition | Limit | Regulatory basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | Canada — Radiation Emitting Devices Regulations, Part III (Microwave Ovens), with the prescribed test load in place | 1.0 mW/cm2 | C.R.C., c. 1370, s. 4(1)(a)(i): leakage radiation at all points at least 5 cm from the external surface shall not exceed 1.0 mW/cm2 with the test load prescribed by s. 4(3)(a) placed in the centre of the shelf in the cavity for a cooking oven with total microwave power generating capacity not greater than 1.5 kW (or as specified by the manufacturer for other ovens) |
| (b) | United States — 21 CFR 1030.10, measured prior to acquisition by a purchaser | 1 mW/cm2 | 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1): equivalent plane-wave power density shall not exceed 1 milliwatt per square centimeter at any point 5 centimeters or more from the external surface of the oven, measured prior to acquisition by a purchaser |
| (c) | United States — 21 CFR 1030.10, after acquisition by a purchaser | 5 mW/cm2 | 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1): 'and, thereafter, 5 milliwatts per square centimeter at any such point' |

CANADA — DETAIL

Governing provision: Radiation Emitting Devices Regulations, C.R.C., c. 1370, s. 4(1)(a), as published by the Department of Justice (current consolidation fetched for this work). The relevant text is:

'4 (1) Every microwave oven shall, when fully assembled and operating with its service controls and user controls adjusted to yield the maximum output, function in such a manner that (a) the leakage radiation, measured with the instrument prescribed by paragraph (3)(b), at all points at least 5 cm from the external surface of the oven, does not exceed (i) 1.0 mW/cm2 with the test load prescribed by paragraph (3)(a) placed (A) in the centre of the shelf in the cavity, in the case of an oven that is designed for cooking and that has a total microwave power generating capacity not greater than 1.5 kW, and (B) as specified by the manufacturer, in the case of an oven other than an oven described in clause (A), and (ii) 5.0 mW/cm2 without a test load, where the oven is operable in such conditions...'

The prescribed test load for an ordinary domestic cooking oven of not greater than 1.5 kW total microwave power generating capacity is 275 ± 15 mL of water at an initial temperature of 20 ± 5 °C, per s. 4(3)(a)(i). Therefore the answer to ask (a) is 1.0 mW/cm2.

Important adjacent Canadian condition, not the answer to (a) but part of the same design file: if the oven is operable without a test load, s. 4(1)(a)(ii) separately requires that leakage not exceed 5.0 mW/cm2 without a test load. The question asks for the with-load condition, so the reported Canadian value is 1.0 mW/cm2.

UNITED STATES — DETAIL

Governing provision: 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1). The relevant text is:

'(1) Power density limit. The equivalent plane-wave power density existing in the proximity of the external oven surface shall not exceed 1 milliwatt per square centimeter at any point 5 centimeters or more from the external surface of the oven, measured prior to acquisition by a purchaser, and, thereafter, 5 milliwatts per square centimeter at any such point.'

Thus:
- Ask (b), pre-acquisition: 1 mW/cm2.
- Ask (c), post-acquisition: 5 mW/cm2.

The US limit is an equivalent plane-wave power density. The quoted provision does not impose the Canadian 'test load in place' condition as part of the limit paragraph; the US measurement and test conditions are in 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(3), including measurement through at least one stirrer cycle and accounting for measurement errors and uncertainties. The limit values themselves are 1 mW/cm2 before acquisition and 5 mW/cm2 thereafter.

DUAL-MARKET DESIGN CONSEQUENCE

A single oven shipped to both markets must satisfy the stricter applicable limit at all points at least 5 cm from the external surface: 1.0 mW/cm2. That is the Canadian with-test-load limit and the US pre-acquisition limit. The US post-acquisition 5 mW/cm2 value does not permit the as-manufactured oven to exceed 1 mW/cm2 before acquisition; it is the limit that applies after the oven has been acquired by a purchaser.

Do not use the US 5 mW/cm2 post-acquisition figure as the production design target. Do not use the Canadian 5.0 mW/cm2 no-load figure as the answer to the with-load question. The correct three answers are 1.0 mW/cm2, 1 mW/cm2, and 5 mW/cm2 for (a), (b), and (c) respectively.

# Noise exposure limit and action values, and the treatment of hearing protection (Great Britain)

Regime: The Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 (SI 2005/1643), in force for general industry in Great Britain from 6 April 2006 (music and entertainment 6 April 2008). Enforced by HSE / local authorities under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. (Northern Ireland has parallel 2006 Regulations with the same values; the EU parent instrument, Directive 2003/10/EC, also uses the same numbers, so the GB answer is unchanged by the GB/EU divergence.)

## 1. The legal values (regulation 4)

| Value | Daily or weekly personal noise exposure, LEP,d / LEP,w | Peak sound pressure, LCpeak |
|---|---|---|
| Lower exposure action value (reg 4(1)) | **80 dB(A)** | **135 dB(C)** |
| Upper exposure action value (reg 4(2)) | **85 dB(A)** | **137 dB(C)** |
| **Exposure limit value (reg 4(3))** | **87 dB(A)** | **140 dB(C)** |

The **exposure limit value** the employer asked for is therefore:

- **87 dB(A)** daily or weekly personal noise exposure; and
- **140 dB(C)** peak sound pressure.

Regulation 4(3) verbatim: "The exposure limit values are - (a) a daily or weekly personal noise exposure of 87 dB (A-weighted); and (b) a peak sound pressure of 140 dB (C-weighted)."

Notes on the numbers:

- These are the *only* legal exposure limit values. There is no separate GB value for, e.g., impulsive noise; the peak value covers it.
- The dB(A) value is an 8-hour-energy-equivalent daily dose (or a 5-day energy average if weekly averaging is lawfully used). It is not a spot sound level: a task at 95 dB(A) for 45 minutes contributes far less than 95 dB(A) to the daily figure.
- The peak value is a true instantaneous maximum, C-weighted, per Schedule 2 to the Regulations - not an Leq and not averaged over the day.
- The ELV is a ceiling that must not be exceeded, not a target. Complying with it does not discharge the separate general duty in regulation 6(1) to reduce exposure to as low a level as is reasonably practicable, by means other than hearing protection.
- Breaching the ELV is a breach of the Regulations; it is not a permissible operating condition.

## 2. May hearing-protector attenuation be counted against the upper exposure action value?

**No.**

Regulation 4(5) verbatim: "In applying the exposure limit values in paragraph (3), **but not in applying the lower and upper exposure action values in paragraphs (1) and (2)**, account shall be taken of the protection given to the employee by any personal hearing protectors provided by the employer in accordance with regulation 7(2)."

HSE *Controlling noise at work* (L108), paragraphs 30-31, states the same rule:

- para 30: "When considering lower and upper EAVs you must not take account of the reduction of noise provided by wearing hearing protection."
- para 31: "When considering the ELVs you should take account of the reduction of noise provided by wearing hearing protection. At or above an upper EAV hearing protection must be provided and worn. This hearing protection must be sufficient to reduce noise at the ear to below the ELVs (see regulation 7)."

HSE *Noise at work: A brief guide* (INDG362) repeats it: "Do not make any allowance for the wearing of personal hearing protection when you estimate workers' noise exposure levels."

So the decision sequence is:

1. Measure/estimate LEP,d (or LEP,w) and LCpeak **with no allowance for protectors**.
2. Compare those unprotected figures with 80/135 and 85/137 to determine which action values are reached or exceeded and therefore which duties are triggered.
3. Only when checking the ELV do you subtract the attenuation the protectors actually give, and confirm the level **at the ear** is not above 87 dB(A) / 140 dB(C).

A protector never moves an employee from "above the upper EAV" to "below the upper EAV". If the unprotected exposure is 90 dB(A), the upper EAV is exceeded and every upper-EAV duty applies, whatever the protector's SNR.

### Duties that follow (why the distinction matters)

- **At/above lower EAV (80 dB(A) / 135 dB(C))**: make hearing protectors available on request (reg 7(1)); provide information, instruction and training (reg 8); ensure protectors are used properly; health surveillance where the risk assessment shows it is required (reg 9); mark hearing protection zones where reasonably practicable.
- **At/above upper EAV (85 dB(A) / 137 dB(C))**: if noise cannot be reduced below the upper EAV by other means, personal hearing protectors must be provided and their use **mandatory** (reg 7(2)); the area must be designated a Hearing Protection Zone, demarcated with the Schedule 1 Part II para 3.3 sign, access restricted where practicable, and no employee may enter unless wearing protectors (reg 7(3)); health surveillance (hearing checks) for those regularly exposed (reg 9); information/instruction/training (reg 8).
- **ELV (87 dB(A) / 140 dB(C))**: must not be exceeded at the ear after taking account of protection actually provided and worn. If it would be exceeded, the protection is inadequate or not being worn correctly - take immediate action (better/other protectors, reduced exposure time, engineered control), because the limit is absolute.

## 3. Practical procedure for the employer

**Step 1 - Determine the metric.** Use daily personal noise exposure LEP,d unless exposure varies markedly from day to day, in which case weekly averaging (LEP,w) may be used (reg 4(4)). Weekly averaging is an option, not a default, and HSE L108 para 29 requires that it does not increase risk (it is not acceptable to use it to expose anyone to very high levels on a single day without protection), that the workforce and safety representatives are consulted, and that workers are told its purpose and effects. Determine LCpeak separately regardless.

**Step 2 - Compute without protection.**
- LEP,d = LAeq,Te + 10 log10(Te / 8), with Te in hours; for multiple tasks sum the exposure contributions (energy summation, or use HSE's daily noise exposure calculator).
- LEP,w = 10 log10[ (1/5) x SUM over the week of 10^(0.1 x LEP,d,i) ].
- LCpeak from the maximum C-weighted instantaneous pressure per Schedule 2.

**Step 3 - Compare unprotected figures with 80/85 dB(A) and 135/137 dB(C)** and record which action values are reached or exceeded. No protector credit at this step.

**Step 4 - Select protectors (reg 7(4)-(5)).** Suitability, comfort, compatibility with other PPE, and adequate attenuation without over-protection. HSE guidance: choose protectors that bring the level at the ear below 85 dB(A) (and in any event below the 87 dB(A) ELV), but avoid reducing it below 70 dB(A) at the ear, which causes communication and warning-signal problems and leads people to remove the protector. Use the manufacturer's SNR/HML/octave-band data and HSE's hearing protection calculator; the single-number SNR guide is not suitable where the noise has significant low-frequency content.

**Step 5 - Check the ELV at the ear.** Subtract the assumed protection (e.g. SNR method L' = L - SNR, or the HML/octave-band method) and confirm L' <= 87 dB(A) and L'Cpeak <= 140 dB(C). Record the calculation.

**Worked illustration (for orientation only, not a real assessment):** measured LEP,d = 90 dB(A); protectors with 12 dB assumed protection. Against the action values, use 90 dB(A) - above the 85 dB(A) upper EAV, so protectors are mandatory, the area is a Hearing Protection Zone, and health surveillance applies. Against the ELV, 90 - 12 = 78 dB(A) at the ear, below 87 dB(A) - compliant, provided the protectors are worn correctly at all times in the noisy environment. Removing them for even a few minutes materially reduces the real protection and can put the ear back above the ELV.

**Step 6 - Manage and review.** Ensure protectors are worn at all times in the noisy environment, correctly fitted (long hair, woolly hats, spectacles, earrings all compromise the seal), stored and maintained; train users in fitting, use, care, and reporting damage/replacement (reg 8, reg 7(6)); review the assessment on change and in any event at intervals of about two years or less (reg 5).

## 4. Direct answers

1. **Legal exposure limit values: 87 dB(A) daily or weekly personal noise exposure, and 140 dB(C) peak sound pressure** (Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, reg 4(3)). For completeness the action values are 80/135 dB (lower) and 85/137 dB (upper) in the same units.
2. **No.** The attenuation of hearing protectors the employer has issued **must not be counted** when judging whether the upper exposure action value has been reached or exceeded (reg 4(5); L108 paras 30-31; INDG362). Protector attenuation is counted **only** when checking compliance with the 87 dB(A) / 140 dB(C) exposure limit values, at the ear.

# Rydberg constant R∞: CODATA 2022 recommended value, its standard uncertainty, and the CODATA 2018 value it replaced

## 1. Answers (as published by NIST, not re-rounded)

| # | Quantity | Value (NIST display form) | Machine form | Unit | Relative std. uncertainty |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | R∞, CODATA 2022 recommended value | 10 973 731.568 157 | 10973731.568157 | m^-1 | 1.1 × 10^-12 |
| 2 | Standard uncertainty of the 2022 value (k = 1) | 0.000 012 | 0.000012 | m^-1 | — |

Context for ask 3 (not a separate ask, given so the 2018 entry is usable): the 2018 standard uncertainty is 0.000 021 m^-1, published in concise form as 10 973 731.568 160(21) m^-1.

Concise forms exactly as NIST prints them:

- 2022: `10 973 731.568 157(12)  m^-1`
- 2018: `10 973 731.568 160(21)  m^-1`

- Uncertainty quoted to two significant digits, aligned to the last two digits of the value (positions 6 of the decimals). Do not present the 2022 uncertainty as "1.2 × 10^-5" in a context where that reads as one significant digit; NIST's own digits are 0.000 012.

- NIST footnote carried with the unit: "The full description of unit m^-1 is cycles or periods per meter." If angular wavenumber (rad m^-1) is wanted, that is a different quantity and would require an explicit 2π conversion; the values above must not be silently converted.

## 3. Provenance (source of record and retrieval)

Cite as: NIST, CODATA Internationally Recommended 2022 Values of the Fundamental Physical Constants (physics.nist.gov/constants), value retrieved 2026-11-18.

## 4. Verification performed on these numbers

1. Two-source agreement. The 2022 value and uncertainty appear identically on the CODATA constant page and in the allascii table; the 2018 value and uncertainty appear identically on the SP 961 wall chart and in the 2018 extensive listing. No transcription discrepancy.

## 5. 2018 → 2022 change (reported, not interpreted)
