# Microwave oven leakage limits — Canada vs. US, one SKU, both markets

## 0. Answer

| Sub-question | Jurisdiction / condition | Limit at points ≥ 5 cm from the external surface | Value (mW/cm2) |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | Canada — Radiation Emitting Devices Regulations, C.R.C., c. 1370, Part III (Microwave Ovens), s. 4(1)(a)(i), **with the prescribed test load in place** | 1.0 mW/cm2 | **1.0** |
| (b) | US — 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1), **measured prior to acquisition by a purchaser** | 1 mW/cm2 | **1** |
| (c) | US — 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1), **thereafter** (after acquisition by a purchaser) | 5 mW/cm2 | **5** |

All three are already expressed in mW/cm2 in the regulatory text; no unit conversion is required. (Results entries 1, 2 and 3 above correspond to sub-questions (a), (b) and (c).)

Equivalent expressions for the same numbers, for meter/field-strength work:
- 1 mW/cm2 = 10 W/m2 ≡ 61.4 V/m rms equivalent plane-wave field (E = sqrt(Pd × 377); sqrt(10 × 377) = 61.4).
- 5 mW/cm2 = 50 W/m2 ≡ 137.3 V/m rms (sqrt(50 × 377) = 137.3).
- "Equivalent plane-wave power density" is defined in both regimes as the square of the rms electric field divided by the impedance of free space, 377 ohms (21 CFR 1030.10(b)(8)).

## 1. Governing text, quoted

### (a) Canada — C.R.C., c. 1370, Radiation Emitting Devices Regulations, Part III

Section 4(1)(a), verbatim:

> "4 (1) Every microwave oven shall, when fully assembled and operating with its service controls and user controls adjusted to yield the maximum output, function in such a manner that
> (a) the leakage radiation, measured with the instrument prescribed by paragraph (3)(b), at all points at least 5 cm from the external surface of the oven, does not exceed
> (i) **1.0 mW/cm2 with the test load prescribed by paragraph (3)(a) placed**
> (A) in the centre of the shelf in the cavity, in the case of an oven that is designed for cooking and that has a total microwave power generating capacity not greater than 1.5 kW, and
> (B) as specified by the manufacturer, in the case of an oven other than an oven described in clause (A), and
> (ii) 5.0 mW/cm2 without a test load, where the oven is operable in such conditions; and
> (b) the intensity of X-ray exposure, at 5 cm from the external surface of the oven, does not exceed 0.5 mR per hour spread over an area of 10 cm2."

Section 4(3), verbatim, defining the load and the instrument:

> "(3) For the purposes of subsections (1) and (2),
> (a) the test load shall be
> (i) in the case of an oven that is designed for cooking and that has a total microwave power generating capacity not greater than 1.5 kW, **275 ± 15 ml of water at an initial temperature of 20 ± 5 °C**, and
> (ii) in the case of an oven other than an oven described in subparagraph (i), the substance and amount thereof specified by the manufacturer as the load to be used for testing the oven; and
> (b) the instrument used to measure leakage radiation shall
> (i) be capable of measuring a power density of 1.0 mW/cm2 with an accuracy of 2 dB or better, and
> (ii) have an indicator with a response time not greater than 3 seconds."

Note the Canadian structure: **two** limits, selected by load condition, not by ownership — 1.0 mW/cm2 with load, 5.0 mW/cm2 without load. The 5.0 figure in Canada is *not* a post-sale relief; do not conflate it with the US 5 mW/cm2.

### (b)/(c) United States — 21 CFR 1030.10

Section 1030.10(c)(1), verbatim:

> "(1) Power density limit. The equivalent plane-wave power density existing in the proximity of the external oven surface shall not exceed **1 milliwatt per square centimeter at any point 5 centimeters or more from the external surface of the oven, measured prior to acquisition by a purchaser, and, thereafter, 5 milliwatts per square centimeter at any such point.**"

Measurement and test conditions, § 1030.10(c)(3), verbatim:

> "(i) Compliance with the power density limit in paragraph (c)(1) of this section shall be determined by measurement of the equivalent plane-wave power density made with an instrument which reaches 90 percent of its steady-state reading within 3 seconds, when the system is subjected to a step-function input signal. Tests for compliance shall account for all measurement errors and uncertainties to ensure that the equivalent plane-wave power density does not exceed the limit prescribed by paragraph (c)(1) of this section.
> (ii) Microwave ovens shall be in compliance with the power density limits if the maximum reading obtained at the location of greatest microwave radiation emission, taking into account all measurement errors and uncertainties, does not exceed the limit specified in paragraph (c)(1) of this section, when the emission is measured through at least one stirrer cycle. As provided by § 1010.13 of this chapter, a manufacturer may request alternative test procedures if, as a result of the stirrer characteristics of a microwave oven, such oven is not susceptible to testing by the procedures described in this paragraph."

"External surface" is defined at § 1030.10(b)(7): "the outside surface of the cabinet or enclosure provided by the manufacturer as part of the microwave oven, **including doors, door handles, latches, and control knobs**."

## 2. Why (b) and (c) differ — and why (c) is not a design target

The US standard is deliberately two-tiered:

- **1 mW/cm2** is the limit that applies to the oven *as it enters commerce* — i.e., the manufacturer's/distributor's obligation. It is the number a new unit must meet at the factory gate and at retail before a purchaser takes delivery.
- **5 mW/cm2** applies "thereafter" — after acquisition by a purchaser, for the life of the oven in the field. It accommodates wear and degradation that a manufacturer cannot control: door gasket compression set, hinge and latch wear, door sag misalignment, seal-surface contamination, and abuse. It is a *field* ceiling, not a manufacturing tolerance.

Consequences to bake into the programme:
1. A new oven at retail must meet **1 mW/cm2**, not 5.
2. The 5 mW/cm2 number is not available as design margin at the factory gate.
3. A unit that leaves the factory at, say, 3 mW/cm2 is non-compliant even though it is under the post-acquisition figure.
4. Because Canada's 1.0 mW/cm2 is not conditioned on ownership, the **binding limit for a dual-market SKU is 1.0 mW/cm2 in both countries** — the same number, so a single verification report serves both, provided it also records the Canadian load specification and the Canadian no-load result.

## 3. Measurement-conditions matrix (differences that change the test, not the number)

| Condition | Canada, C.R.C. c. 1370 s. 4 | US, 21 CFR 1030.10(c) | Action for one test programme |
|---|---|---|---|
| Distance | "at all points at least 5 cm from the external surface" | "at any point 5 centimeters or more from the external surface" | Identical. Probe datum = 5.0 cm from the **outermost** external surface. |
| Datum for "external surface" | Not defined in the retrieved Part III excerpt | Explicitly includes doors, handles, latches, control knobs (b)(7) | Use the US definition for both; confirm against the Canadian Part III definitions before finalizing the report (see §7). |
| Instrument accuracy | Must be capable of measuring 1.0 mW/cm2 with **accuracy 2 dB or better** (4(3)(b)(i)) | Must **account for all measurement errors and uncertainties** (c)(3)(i) | Use a calibrated meter materially better than 2 dB and publish an uncertainty budget. See margin math in §4. |
| Instrument response | Indicator response time **≤ 3 s** (4(3)(b)(ii)) | Reaches **90 % of steady state within 3 s** for a step-function input (c)(3)(i) | One meter satisfies both if its 90 %-settling spec is ≤ 3 s. |
| Spatial averaging | Max reading; no stirrer-cycle clause in the retrieved text | **Maximum reading** at the location of greatest emission, measured through **at least one stirrer cycle** (c)(3)(ii) | Scan through ≥ 1 full stirrer/turntable cycle and hold the peak; this satisfies both. |
| Test load | **275 ± 15 mL water at 20 ± 5 °C**, placed in the **centre of the shelf**, for cooking ovens with total microwave power generating capacity ≤ 1.5 kW; otherwise manufacturer-specified load (4(3)(a)) | Not specified in the retrieved (c)(3) text — the load used in FDA/CDRH compliance testing comes from the agency's test/compliance procedure, not from the quoted standard | Run the Canadian load as the primary condition; confirm the CDRH test load against current FDA guidance before signing the report. |
| Control settings | "fully assembled and operating with its service controls and user controls adjusted to yield the maximum output" (4(1)) | Implied by the limit; not restated in (c)(3) | Test at maximum output, highest rated line voltage, stabilized magnetron temperature. |
| No-load condition | **5.0 mW/cm2 without a test load**, where the oven is operable in such conditions (4(1)(a)(ii)) | No separate no-load provision in the retrieved text | **Additional Canadian-only test.** Required for the Canadian submission. |
| X-ray | 0.5 mR/h at 5 cm over 10 cm2 (4(1)(b)) | Not limited by 1030.10 | Canadian-only test; include on the same report. |

## 4. Engineering the design margin (the number that actually matters)

The Canadian instrument specification is only "2 dB or better." 2 dB in power is a factor of 10^(2/10) = **1.585**. That cuts both ways:

- A meter that **under-reads** by 2 dB will display 1.00 mW/cm2 for a true 1.58 mW/cm2. An indicated 1.00 therefore does **not** prove compliance to 1.0.
- To *demonstrate* true ≤ 1.0 mW/cm2 with a meter known only to ±2 dB, the indicated reading must be ≤ 1.0 / 1.585 = **0.63 mW/cm2**.
- Similarly, to demonstrate true ≤ 5.0 mW/cm2 (post-acquisition, or the Canadian no-load condition) with such a meter, indicated must be ≤ 5.0 / 1.585 = **3.15 mW/cm2**.

Recommended programme limits:

| Quantity | Regulatory limit | Meter-spec-limited demonstration threshold | Recommended internal design/verification target |
|---|---|---|---|
| With-load leakage, new unit (CA + US pre-acquisition) | 1.0 mW/cm2 | ≤ 0.63 mW/cm2 indicated on a ±2 dB meter | **≤ 0.50 mW/cm2** max over all surfaces, with a calibrated meter whose documented uncertainty is ≤ ±0.5 dB |
| No-load leakage (Canada only) | 5.0 mW/cm2 | ≤ 3.15 mW/cm2 indicated on a ±2 dB meter | **≤ 3.0 mW/cm2** |

A 0.50 mW/cm2 ceiling gives 6 dB of margin to the 1.0 limit, absorbs unit-to-unit seal variation, and survives the ±2 dB worst-case instrument tolerance without argument. Do not design to 1.0.

## 5. Executable test procedure (one run, both markets)

1. **Instrument.** Calibrated broadband microwave leakage meter, probe area ≤ 2 cm2 (e.g., 5 cm2 max per typical isotropic probes), 90 %-settling ≤ 3 s, certificate traceable and within its calibration interval. Record calibration ID, date, and uncertainty.
2. **DUT conditioning.** Fully assembled as shipped, including handles, knobs, and any user-installed parts that ship attached. Stabilize at room temperature. Record model, serial, rated microwave power, and whether total generating capacity is ≤ 1.5 kW (decides the Canadian load clause).
3. **Load (Canadian condition and primary run).** 275 ± 15 mL of potable water at 20 ± 5 °C in a low-loss (glass/plastic) vessel, placed in the **centre of the shelf**. Record actual volume and initial temperature.
4. **Power-up.** Maximum output, highest rated line voltage for the market, controls at maximum. Allow the magnetron to reach thermal steady state before recording peaks.
5. **Scan.** Probe standoff held at 5.0 cm from the **outermost** external surface. Survey all six faces on a grid no coarser than 5 cm, with denser scanning (≤ 2 cm pitch) at: door perimeter and all four door seams, latch/handle region, hinge line, waveguide/cover plate, ventilation grille, control panel, rear panel, and the bottom if the unit is so designed. Keep scanning through at least one complete stirrer/turntable cycle at each candidate hotspot; hold and record the **maximum** reading.
6. **Record** the peak location, the peak reading, and the local ambient. Apply the documented measurement uncertainty in the direction that is conservative for the limit.
7. **No-load run (Canada only, if the oven is operable with an empty cavity).** Repeat steps 4–6 with the cavity empty. Compare against 5.0 mW/cm2.
8. **X-ray run (Canada only).** Measure at 5 cm from the external surface; limit 0.5 mR/h averaged over 10 cm2.
9. **Verdict.** Pass/fail against 1.0 mW/cm2 (with load) and 5.0 mW/cm2 (no load), applying the uncertainty budget — not against 5 mW/cm2 for the with-load case.

## 6. Common errors this design review is guarding against

- **Quoting 5 mW/cm2 as the US design limit.** It applies only "thereafter," after a purchaser has acquired the oven. A new unit must meet 1 mW/cm2.
- **Quoting Canada as 5 mW/cm2.** The Canadian 5.0 mW/cm2 is a *no-load* limit, not a post-sale limit, and it sits in the same subparagraph as the 1.0 figure, which makes the misread easy.
- **Assuming the two countries share one test method because they share one number.** They share the number; they do not share the no-load requirement (Canada-only), the X-ray requirement (Canada-only), or the stirrer-cycle averaging clause (US-only).
- **Measuring 5 cm from the cabinet skin** rather than from the outermost protrusion. Under the US definition, the handle and knobs are part of the external surface, so the 5 cm envelope follows them.
- **Ignoring measurement uncertainty.** The US text requires it explicitly (c)(3)(i); a bare peak reading is not a compliance demonstration.
- **Using a slow detector.** Both regimes impose a 3 s criterion; a peak-hold meter with a slow thermal head can under-report the true maximum through a stirrer cycle.

## 7. Currency and residual verification items

- **Canada.** Text cited from the consolidation in force 2025-10-09 to 2026-10-29 (last amended 2025-10-09). The identical 1.0 mW/cm2 / 5.0 mW/cm2 / 275 ± 15 mL wording also appears in the archived 2018-04-04 consolidation, so the value is stable and is not an artifact of a recent amendment.
- **US.** The eCFR current text and the 2024 printed CFR (title 21, volume 8, § 1030.10) agree verbatim on (c)(1) and (c)(3). No pending amendment affects the values.
- **Residual items to close before the report is signed (do not change the three numbers above):**
  1. Confirm the Canadian Part III definition of "external surface" (not present in the retrieved excerpt) — it is expected to align with the US definition but should be quoted in the report.
  2. Confirm the test load used in current FDA/CDRH microwave-oven compliance testing, since § 1030.10(c)(3) as retrieved specifies instrument response and stirrer-cycle averaging but not the load itself.
  3. Confirm whether the Canadian Part III text contains any acquisition-conditional provision; none appears in the retrieved text, so the 1.0 mW/cm2 limit should be treated as unconditional.

question: X32
shape: Occupational noise, Great Britain statutory instrument
answer:
ADVICE NOTE — STATUTORY NOISE EXPOSURE LIMIT VALUES AND THE USE OF HEARING-PROTECTOR ATTENUATION
Legal basis: Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 (SI 2005/1643), as they apply in Great Britain (England, Wales, Scotland). In force 6 April 2006 for general industry, including manufacturing (6 April 2008 for the music and entertainment sectors). They replaced the Noise at Work Regulations 1989; the old 90 dB(A) action level is no longer law and must not be used.

1. SHORT ANSWERS
Q1 — The exposure limit values (reg 4(3)) are: 87 dB(A) daily or weekly personal noise exposure, and 140 dB(C) peak sound pressure.
Q2 — No. The attenuation given by hearing protectors you have issued may NOT be counted when judging whether the upper exposure action value has been reached. It may only be counted when testing compliance with the exposure limit values.

2. THE THREE TIERS OF VALUE UNDER REGULATION 4
| Tier | Daily or weekly personal noise exposure — LEX,8h / LEX,40h | Peak sound pressure — LCpeak |
|---|---|---|
| Lower exposure action value — reg 4(1) | 80 dB(A) | 135 dB(C) |
| Upper exposure action value — reg 4(2) | 85 dB(A) | 137 dB(C) |
| Exposure limit value — reg 4(3) | 87 dB(A) | 140 dB(C) |

Notes on how the quantities are defined:
- 'Daily personal noise exposure' is the A-weighted, 8-hour-normalised daily noise dose (LEX,8h), ascertained under Schedule 1 Part 1 — a combination of how loud and how long, across all noise in the working day, not a spot reading.
- 'Weekly personal noise exposure' (LEX,40h) is ascertained under Schedule 1 Part 2. Regulation 4(4) permits weekly averaging in place of daily exposure only 'where the exposure of an employee to noise varies markedly from day to day'. It is an election for genuine day-to-day variation, not a routine smoothing device; HSE guidance (L108) advises consulting the workers and their safety representatives on whether weekly averaging is appropriate and explaining its purpose and effects. The overriding duty to reduce risk to as low as is reasonably practicable (reg 6(1)) is unaffected by the election.
- 'Peak sound pressure' is the maximum C-weighted instantaneous sound pressure (LCpeak), ascertained under Schedule 2 — the true peak, not the maximum Fast or Slow time-weighted level.

3. THE RULE ON HEARING-PROTECTOR ATTENUATION (the answer to Q2)
Regulation 4(5) states: 'In applying the exposure limit values in paragraph (3), but not in applying the lower and upper exposure action values in paragraphs (1) and (2), account shall be taken of the protection given to the employee by any personal hearing protectors provided by the employer in accordance with regulation 7(2).'
HSE's Approved Code of Practice/guidance L108 confirms at paragraphs 30–31: when considering the lower and upper exposure action values you must not take account of the reduction in noise provided by wearing hearing protection; when considering the exposure limit values you should.
Consequences you must build into your assessment method:
(a) The 85 dB(A) / 137 dB(C) upper exposure action value test is made on the UNPROTECTED exposure. If unprotected exposure is at or above 85 dB(A) or 137 dB(C), the upper EAV is reached — full stop — even if a protector would bring the level at the ear down to 78 dB(A).
(b) The same applies to the 80 dB(A) / 135 dB(C) lower exposure action value.
(c) Only the 87 dB(A) / 140 dB(C) exposure limit value test uses the protected level at the ear.
(d) 'Protection given ... by any personal hearing protectors provided by the employer in accordance with regulation 7(2)' means protectors actually provided and actually worn correctly. A protector on a shelf, or worn intermittently, gives no credit in the ELV calculation; and failure to ensure use is itself a breach of regulation 8.

4. WHAT EACH TIER OBLIGES YOU TO DO (manufacturing site)
At or above the LOWER exposure action values — 80 dB(A) / 135 dB(C) (unprotected):
- Suitable and sufficient risk assessment (reg 5), recorded, identifying the measures needed and any employees requiring health surveillance; review on change and at reasonable intervals (HSE suggests not more than about two years).
- Make personal hearing protectors available on request to exposed employees (reg 7(1)).
- Provide information, instruction and training (reg 10).
- Reduce risk by means other than PPE so far as reasonably practicable (reg 6).
At or above the UPPER exposure action values — 85 dB(A) / 137 dB(C) (unprotected):
- All of the above, plus a planned programme of noise control at source (reg 6).
- Provide personal hearing protectors and ensure they are used properly (reg 7(2), reg 8).
- Designate, demarcate and sign Hearing Protection Zones with the mandatory ear-protection sign, and restrict access where practicable and justified (reg 7(3)).
- Provide health surveillance (hearing checks/audiometry) for employees identified by the risk assessment, in particular those regularly exposed at or above the upper EAV (reg 9).
Against the EXPOSURE LIMIT VALUES — 87 dB(A) / 140 dB(C) (protected level, i.e. after crediting protector attenuation):
- These are limits that must not be exceeded. HSE guidance (L108 para 31) is that at or above an upper EAV protectors must be provided and worn, and must be sufficient to reduce the noise at the ear below the exposure limit values. Complying with the ELVs is a separate duty from, and does not discharge, the duty to reduce risk so far as is reasonably practicable.

5. METHOD FOR APPLYING PROTECTOR ATTENUATION (ELV TEST ONLY)
Step 1 — Establish the unprotected LEX,8h (or LEX,40h) and LCpeak by measurement or reliable estimation, by a competent person, using suitably calibrated equipment and representative sampling of the actual working day.
Step 2 — Compare the unprotected figures with 80/135 and 85/137. Those comparisons fix your action-value duties. Do not subtract anything at this step.
Step 3 — Select a protector and calculate the assumed protection at the ear using a standardised method: BS EN ISO 4869-2 (octave-band, HML or SNR method), or HSE's published hearing protection calculator, using the manufacturer's test data for that exact model.
Step 4 — Protected exposure = unprotected exposure minus the calculated assumed attenuation. Compare with 87 dB(A) and 140 dB(C). If the protected level is at or above either figure, the protector is inadequate and the exposure is unlawful — change the protector, the duration, or (preferably) the engineering control.
Step 5 — Check for over-protection: HSE guidance is that protectors reducing the level at the ear below about 70 dB should be avoided, because over-protection impairs communication and the hearing of warning signals and tends to lead to protectors being removed. A sensible design band at the ear is therefore roughly 70–85 dB(A).
Step 6 — Assess peak (LCpeak) attenuation separately. Protectors attenuate peaks less reliably than continuous noise, and the C-weighted peak must be addressed in its own right against 140 dB(C); do not assume the continuous-noise attenuation figure applies unchanged.
Step 7 — Treat calculated attenuation as an assumption, not a guarantee. Real-world protection is commonly lower than laboratory rating; consider derating and, more importantly, verify fit, condition and wearing time by supervision and observation.

6. WORKED EXAMPLE (illustrative figures only — not a site assessment)
An operator's unprotected daily personal noise exposure is established as LEX,8h = 90 dB(A).
- Against the upper EAV: 90 dB(A) is at or above 85 dB(A), so the upper exposure action value is reached, and the full upper-tier package (noise-control programme, mandatory protectors, Hearing Protection Zone, health surveillance) applies. The fact that a protector might bring the level at the ear to 75 dB(A) does not change this — reg 4(5) forbids crediting it here.
- Against the ELV: the selected protector yields an assumed attenuation of 15 dB at the ear. Protected exposure = 90 − 15 = 75 dB(A), which is below the 87 dB(A) exposure limit value, so the ELV is met on this protector. The same figure, 75 dB(A), is above the 70 dB(A) over-protection floor, so the protector is not over-protecting.
- Peak: the measured LCpeak must be compared with 137 dB(C) (unprotected) and 140 dB(C) (protected) on its own calculation.

7. COMMON ERRORS THIS RULE IS DESIGNED TO CATCH
- Subtracting a protector's SNR from the measured level and then concluding the upper EAV is not reached. This is a breach of reg 4(5) and is the single most frequent error in manufacturing noise assessments.
- Using the 1989 Regulations' 90 dB(A) action level or 85 dB(A) 'second action level'.
- Defaulting to weekly averaging to bring a daily exposure under 85 dB(A) where exposure does not vary markedly day to day.
- Treating 87 dB(A) as an action value rather than an absolute limit.
- Relying on hearing protection as a substitute for engineering and organisational noise control (reg 6; HSE: protection is for residual risk and as a short-term measure while other controls are developed).
- Equating the catalogue SNR with the protection actually achieved in use.

8. SCOPE, CAVEATS AND JURISDICTION
- This is general compliance information, not a site-specific noise assessment: no workplace measurements were supplied, and the figures above are statutory values that do not vary with your process.
- The values in reg 4 have not been changed since the Regulations came into force; they are the current law in Great Britain.
- Northern Ireland has its own equivalent regulations (separate SI), which carry the same numerical values; if any of your operations are in Northern Ireland, confirm the applicable instrument before relying on this note. The Republic of Ireland and EU Member States transpose the same underlying directive values but with their own instruments and enforcement.
- The assessor must be competent (reg 5) and measurements must be representative and reliable; HSE expects the risk assessment to be recorded and reviewed on change or at intervals of roughly two years or less.

RYDBERG CONSTANT R_infinity — CODATA 2022 vs. CODATA 2018 (NIST-published)

1. CODATA 2022 recommended value (current)

   R_infinity = 10 973 731.568 157 m^-1
   Standard uncertainty = 0.000 012 m^-1
   Concise form: 10 973 731.568 157(12) m^-1
   Relative standard uncertainty: 1.1 x 10^-12
   Explicit form: R_infinity = (10 973 731.568 157 +/- 0.000 012) m^-1

The number in parentheses, (12), is the one-sigma (1 sigma) standard uncertainty in the last two digits of the stated value, i.e. 0.000 012 m^-1. This is the standard (k = 1) uncertainty, not an expanded uncertainty.

Source: NIST, CODATA Value: Rydberg constant, https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?ryd (source line on the page: 'Source: 2022 CODATA recommended values'). Cross-checked against the NIST 2022 ASCII table, https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants/Table/allascii.txt, line:
   Rydberg constant   10 973 731.568 157   0.000 012   m^-1
Both NIST sources agree digit for digit.

Note on the unit: NIST annotates m^-1 for this constant as 'cycles or periods per meter' (the dagger footnote on the value page). No conversion is required; the requested unit is the published unit.

2. CODATA 2018 recommended value (the set replaced by CODATA 2022)

   R_infinity = 10 973 731.568 160 m^-1
   Standard uncertainty = 0.000 021 m^-1
   Concise form: 10 973 731.568 160(21) m^-1
   Relative standard uncertainty: 1.1 x 10^-12
   Explicit form: R_infinity = (10 973 731.568 160 +/- 0.000 021) m^-1

Source: 2018 CODATA recommended values, NIST SP 959 (June 2019), and the NIST 2018 archived constants table (physics.nist.gov/constants, 2018 archive). The 2018 set is the immediately preceding CODATA adjustment, so it is the value the 2022 set replaced (NIST version history, Version 9.0, 9 May 2024: 'The 2022 values replace the previously recommended 2018 CODATA values, which are available in archived tables').

Independent derivation of the 2018 number from the 2018 wall chart (NIST SP 959, https://physics.nist.gov/pdf/wall_2018.pdf, mirrored at https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=928211), which lists the Rydberg frequency rather than R_infinity itself:

   c R_infinity = 3.289 841 960 2508(64) x 10^15 Hz
   c = 299 792 458 m s^-1 (exact)

   R_infinity = (3.289 841 960 2508 x 10^15 Hz) / (299 792 458 m s^-1)
              = 10 973 731.568 160 m^-1

   u(R_infinity) = (6.4 x 10^3 Hz) / (299 792 458 m s^-1)
                 = 2.1 x 10^-5 m^-1  ->  0.000 021 m^-1

This reproduces the published 2018 entry exactly, so the 2018 value is traceable to the fetched NIST source rather than to memory.

3. Comparison of the two values

   2022 - 2018 = 10 973 731.568 157 - 10 973 731.568 160 = -0.000 003 m^-1
              = -3 x 10^-6 m^-1
   Relative shift = -3 x 10^-6 / 1.097 373 156 816 x 10^7 = -2.7 x 10^-13

   Combined one-sigma uncertainty of the difference (treating the two adjustments as independent):
   sqrt(0.000 012^2 + 0.000 021^2) m^-1 = 0.000 024 m^-1 = 2.4 x 10^-5 m^-1

The shift (-3 x 10^-6 m^-1) is about one eighth of the combined uncertainty (2.4 x 10^-5 m^-1), i.e. the two recommended values are consistent within their uncertainties. The improvement in the uncertainty (0.000 021 -> 0.000 012 m^-1, a factor of about 1.75) is the substantive change between the two adjustments for this constant; the central value moved by less than one part in 10^12.

4. Scope, disambiguation and caveats

- The quantity quoted is R_infinity, the Rydberg constant for infinite nuclear mass. It is NOT the hydrogen Rydberg constant R_H (which carries a small reduced-mass correction, R_H = R_infinity / (1 + m_e/m_p)) and NOT any isotopic variant (R_D, R_T). Any downstream use that needs R_H must apply that correction explicitly.
- The unit is m^-1 as published; the value is not converted to energy, frequency or wavelength here. For reference, the same 2022 adjustment gives R_infinity c = 3.289 841 960 2500(36) x 10^15 Hz and R_infinity hc = 13.605 693 122 990(15) eV (NIST 2022 ASCII table), but these are separate entries and are not the answer to the ask.
- The uncertainty quoted is the CODATA standard (one-sigma) uncertainty. If an expanded uncertainty is required for a regulatory or calibration context, multiply by the coverage factor k (k = 2 gives approximately 95 % coverage for a normal distribution).
- Values are quoted at the full precision published by NIST; no rounding has been applied to either the value or its uncertainty.

5. Citation block (ready to paste)

   Eite Tiesinga, Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, and Barry N. Taylor (2024), 'The 2022 CODATA Recommended Values of the Fundamental Physical Constants' (Web Version 9.0), Database developed by J. Baker, M. Douma, and S. Kotochigova, available at https://physics.nist.gov/constants, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD 20899. [Rydberg constant: https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?ryd]

   P. J. Mohr, D. B. Newell, B. N. Taylor, and E. Tiesinga (2025), 'CODATA Recommended Values of the Fundamental Physical Constants: 2022', Reviews of Modern Physics (NIST publication page: https://www.nist.gov/publications/codata-recommended-values-fundamental-physical-constants-2022; paper: https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=958143).

   For the 2018 set: '2018 CODATA Recommended Values of the Fundamental Physical Constants', NIST SP 959 (June 2019), https://physics.nist.gov/pdf/wall_2018.pdf; full archived table at https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants/ (2018 archive).

6. Verification checklist

   [x] 2022 value and uncertainty taken from the NIST CODATA value page and independently confirmed against the NIST 2022 ASCII table.
   [x] 2018 value confirmed two ways: the published CODATA 2018 entry (10 973 731.568 160(21) m^-1) and a recomputation from the 2018 wall chart's c R_infinity value divided by the exact speed of light.
   [x] Both values are in m^-1 as requested, with no unit conversion.
   [x] Both uncertainties are one-sigma standard uncertainties in the last digits, matching NIST's parenthetical convention.
   [x] R_infinity distinguished from R_H and isotopic Rydberg constants.
   [x] Difference between the two adjustments stated and shown to be within the combined uncertainty.

          to the far side of the traveled way, or to a median of sufficient
          width for pedestrians to wait.
  Step 2. Pedestrian change interval = L / v, with v = 3.5 ft/s by
          default (apply a reduced v per section 4 only where the stated
          conditions are met). Round up to the next whole second as a
          timing-plan practice; the retrieved text does not itself
          prescribe a rounding rule, so record the rounding convention
          used in the timing sheet.
  Step 3. Buffer interval = 2 s minimum (answer #1).
  Step 4. Walk interval = 7 s guidance minimum, or 4 s where the Option
          conditions are met.
  Step 5. Total pedestrian phase = walk + change + buffer. Confirm the
          buffer does not begin later than the beginning of the red
          clearance interval, if a red clearance interval is used.

Worked example (L = 48 ft, default speed, 7 s walk):
  Change interval = 48 / 3.5 = 13.71 s -> 14 s (rounded up)
  Buffer interval = 2 s (minimum; may be longer)
  Walk interval   = 7 s
  Total pedestrian phase = 7 + 14 + 2 = 23 s minimum

Cross-check of the example against the stated bounds: 2 s used equals the
stated minimum (not below it); 3.5 ft/s used is the stated default (not the
4 ft/s evaluation option); 14 s exceeds 13.71 s so no pedestrian is short-
changed by rounding. If the same 48 ft were (incorrectly) sized at 4 ft/s
the change interval would be 12 s and the crossing would be undersized —
this is exactly the error the default in answer #2 guards against.

answer:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — Article 120(3) MDR transitional placement dates, class IIa legacy MDD certificate

DEVICE / LEGAL POSITION TAKEN AS GIVEN
- Certificate issued under Directive 93/42/EEC, class IIa device.
- Certificate still valid by virtue of Article 120(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR).
- The conditions of Article 120(3c) are met.
- Governing text: MDR as amended by Regulation (EU) 2023/1127 (the currently applicable version of Article 120).

=== 1. ANSWERS ===

ASK 1 — Last date on which the legacy device may be placed on the market or put into service:
    31 DECEMBER 2028

ASK 2 — Last date by which a formal application must have been lodged with a notified body:
    26 MAY 2024

ASK 3 — Last date by which a written agreement must have been signed with the notified body:
    26 SEPTEMBER 2024

(Related but not asked: Article 120(3c)(d) required a quality management system in accordance with Article 10(9) to be in place no later than 26 May 2024 — the same date as the application gate.)

=== 2. LEGAL BASIS AND DERIVATION ===

2.1 The placement right — Article 120(3) and (3a)(b)
Article 120(3) provides that, by way of derogation from Article 5 and provided the conditions of Article 120(3c) are met, devices referred to in Article 120(3a) and (3b) may be placed on the market or put into service until the dates set out in those paragraphs.

Article 120(3a) reads: 'Devices which have a certificate that was issued in accordance with Directive 90/385/EEC or Directive 93/42/EEC and that is valid by virtue of paragraph 2 of this Article may be placed on the market or put into service until the following dates: ... (b) 31 December 2028, for class IIb devices other than those covered by point (a) of this paragraph, for class IIa devices, and for class I devices placed on the market in sterile condition or having a measuring function.'

A class IIa device falls expressly within point (b), not point (a). Point (a) — 31 December 2027 — is reserved for class III devices and for class IIb implantable devices other than those covered by the class III custom-made provision. The class assigned by the legacy certificate therefore controls the answer; a device that is in fact class IIb implantable would take 31 December 2027 instead, so the class IIa classification should be evidenced from the certificate itself (the certificate states the class and the Annex/rule under 93/42/EEC) and retained in the technical file.

The date is inclusive: the device may lawfully be placed on the market or put into service on 31 December 2028 itself. From 1 January 2029, placement on the market or putting into service on the basis of the legacy certificate is no longer permitted; an MDR certificate (or a derogation under Article 59(1), or a competent-authority requirement under Article 97(1)) is then required.

2.2 The two procedural gates — Article 120(3c)(e)
Article 120(3c) makes the placement right conditional. Point (e) requires that:
  (i) 'no later than 26 May 2024, the manufacturer, or an authorised representative, has lodged a formal application in accordance with Section 4.3, first subparagraph, of Annex VII for conformity assessment in respect of a device referred to in paragraphs 3b and 3c of this Article or in respect of a device intended to substitute that device'; and
  (ii) 'no later than 26 September 2024 the notified body and the manufacturer have signed a written agreement in accordance with Section 4.3, second subparagraph, of Annex VII.'

Both gates are absolute calendar dates fixed by the Regulation. They are not calculated from the certificate expiry date, from the device class, or from the date of any audit. They are identical for every manufacturer relying on Article 120(3a) or (3b) — the class only changes the end date in 3a/3b, not these two gates.

2.3 Reading of the two gates
- 'Formal application ... in accordance with Section 4.3, first subparagraph, of Annex VII' means the MDR Annex VII application for conformity assessment by a notified body, not an enquiry, a quotation request, a pre-submission, or a letter of intent. The application may be lodged by the manufacturer or by its authorised representative.
- The application may cover the device covered by the legacy certificate OR a device intended to substitute that device. A substitution strategy (e.g. the successor model that replaces the legacy device on the same intended purpose) therefore satisfies the gate.
- 'Written agreement ... in accordance with Section 4.3, second subparagraph, of Annex VII' means the signed written agreement between the manufacturer and the notified body setting out the conformity assessment to be carried out — the document that in practice is the notified-body quotation/contract for the MDR assessment. It must be signed by both parties on or before 26 September 2024. A unilateral acceptance, a purchase order, or an unsigned draft does not satisfy the gate.

=== 3. WHAT THE 31 DECEMBER 2028 DATE DOES AND DOES NOT PROHIBIT ===

- It governs first placement on the Union market and first putting into service. A device placed on the market on or before 31 December 2028 may thereafter continue to be made available on the market or put into service. Article 120(4) provides that devices lawfully placed on the market pursuant to Directives 90/385/EEC and 93/42/EEC prior to 26 May 2021, and devices lawfully placed on the market from 26 May 2021 pursuant to Article 120(3), (3a), (3b) and (3f), 'may continue to be made available on the market or put into service' — with no cut-off in that paragraph.
- Consequently, stock already placed on the market before the end date may continue to be distributed, and devices already in use may remain in service and continue to be serviced. The 31 December 2028 date does not require recall, withdrawal from service, or decommissioning.
- Practical corollary: the manufacturer should be able to evidence, for each serial/lot, the date on which the device was first placed on the market (transfer of risk / making available to the distributor or end user), because that date, not the delivery date, determines whether the device falls on the permitted side of the deadline.

=== 4. CONDITIONS THAT MUST CONTINUE TO BE MET (Article 120(3c)) ===

The placement right under 3a(b) exists only 'provided the conditions set out in paragraph 3c are met'. They are continuing conditions, not one-off tests:
  (a) the device continues to comply with Directive 93/42/EEC;
  (b) there are no significant changes in the design and intended purpose;
  (c) the device does not present an unacceptable risk to health or safety or to other aspects of public health protection;
  (d) the QMS in accordance with Article 10(9) was in place no later than 26 May 2024;
  (e) the Annex VII Section 4.3 application was lodged no later than 26 May 2024 and the written agreement signed no later than 26 September 2024.

If any of these ceases to be met, the derogation in Article 120(3) falls away and the device may no longer be placed on the market or put into service on the strength of the legacy certificate — irrespective of how much of the period to 31 December 2028 remains. A significant change in design or intended purpose triggers the need for MDR certification immediately, and the change itself must not be implemented on the strength of the legacy certificate.

Note that Article 120(3) does not defer the MDR requirements on post-market surveillance, market surveillance, vigilance, and registration of economic operators and of devices: under Article 120(3) those MDR requirements apply in place of the corresponding Directive requirements for the whole of the transitional period.

=== 5. TIMING WARNING — THE TWO GATES ARE ALREADY IN THE PAST ===

26 May 2024 and 26 September 2024 have passed. They are not deadlines that can still be met, extended, or cured. If the manufacturer did not lodge the Annex VII Section 4.3 application by 26 May 2024 and did not have a signed written agreement by 26 September 2024, the Article 120(3) derogation is not available and the device may no longer be placed on the market or put into service on the basis of the legacy certificate. In that situation the only routes are an MDR certificate, a Member State derogation under Article 59(1), or a competent-authority requirement/derogation under Article 97(1). The dates above should therefore be read as 'the last permissible dates', to be verified against the manufacturer's own documentary record, not as targets still open.

=== 6. DOCUMENTARY EVIDENCE TO RETAIN ===

Market surveillance authorities may require proof that the transitional period applies. The file should hold, at minimum:
  1. The MDD 93/42/EEC notified-body certificate, showing class IIa, the issuing notified body, the issue date, and the expiry date, together with evidence that it remains valid by virtue of Article 120(2) (no suspension, withdrawal, restriction or lapse).
  2. The dated Annex VII Section 4.3 first-subparagraph application as lodged with the notified body — dated receipt/acknowledgement on or before 26 May 2024, showing the device or its substitute as the subject of the application.
  3. The countersigned Annex VII Section 4.3 second-subparagraph written agreement — both signatures dated on or before 26 September 2024.
  4. Evidence of the Article 10(9) QMS in place on or before 26 May 2024 (certificate or audit report under the applicable standard).
  5. The change-control record demonstrating no significant change in design or intended purpose since the date of application of the MDR, and the risk/PMS/vigilance records showing compliance with MDR Articles 83–86.
  6. A record of the date each device (or lot/serial) was first placed on the market or put into service, to evidence that placement occurred on or before 31 December 2028.

=== 7. SCOPE NOTE ===

This determination is made against the Union-level text of Article 120 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2023/1127. It does not account for any national measure, notified-body contractual term, or competent-authority decision that imposes an earlier date or an additional condition; none is assumed to apply. It is a regulatory position on the dates, not a conformity assessment, and it does not substitute for the notified body's own view of the application's completeness or of whether a given design change is 'significant'.

question: X5
answer:
# LVD Voltage Scope Determination

**Instrument:** Directive 2014/35/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 February 2014 on the harmonisation of the laws of the Member States relating to the making available on the market of electrical equipment designed for use within certain voltage limits (recast), OJ L 96, 29.3.2014, p. 357–374 (CELEX 32014L0035). It repealed Directive 2006/95/EC with effect from 20 April 2016 (Art. 27).

**Answer to ask 1 — the in-scope voltage ratings (Art. 1, second paragraph, verbatim):**

> "This Directive shall apply to electrical equipment designed for use with a voltage rating of between 50 and 1 000 V for alternating current and between 75 and 1 500 V for direct current, other than the equipment and phenomena listed in Annex II."

| Quantity | Lower bound | Upper bound | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rated voltage, alternating current | 50 | 1 000 | V AC |
| Rated voltage, direct current | 75 | 1 500 | V DC |

Both bounds are read as inclusive: a product rated at exactly 50 V AC or exactly 75 V DC is inside; a product rated above 1 000 V AC or above 1 500 V DC is outside (it is not "designed for use within" the band).

**Answer to ask 2 — verdict:** Equipment designed for use at 24 V AC is **outside the scope** of Directive 2014/35/EU on voltage grounds. 24 V AC is below the 50 V AC lower bound by 26 V (24 is 48 % of the threshold, i.e. 52 % below it). The conclusion holds independently on the DC side as well: a 24 V DC rating is below the 75 V DC lower bound by 51 V. Nothing else in the Directive pulls a genuinely all-24 V AC product back in.

---

## 1. Legal basis and version control

- Operative text: Article 1, second paragraph, of Directive 2014/35/EU (quoted above, confirmed identically in the EN and FR Official Journal texts).
- Commission guidance on interpretation: *Guide to the Low Voltage Directive 2014/35/EU*, November 2016, §6 "Which products are covered?" — used below for the rating rules.
- Currency: EUR-Lex shows a consolidated version dated 30/05/2026. The three numbers that decide this question (50, 1 000, 75, 1 500) are unchanged from the original Low Voltage Directive 73/23/EEC through 2006/95/EC to 2014/35/EU, so the determination is insensitive to which consolidation is used.
- UK note (if relevant): the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016 (SI 2016/1101) retain the same 50–1 000 V AC / 75–1 500 V DC bands, so the conclusion is the same for the GB market.

## 2. Rating rules that decide in/out (from Art. 1 and LVD Guide §6)

| Rule | Content | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| R1 — What "voltage rating" means | "Voltage ratings refer to the voltage of the electrical input or output, not to voltages that may appear inside the equipment." | A 24 V AC appliance that internally generates 400 V (e.g. a boost stage, an ignition circuit, a magnetron supply) is still out of scope on the Directive's own reading. Internal voltages are a design-safety matter, not a scoping matter. |
| R2 — Input or output | "Equipment having either a rated input voltage or a rated output voltage (or both) inside this voltage range" is in scope. | A 24 V AC input device with a 230 V AC rated output (inverter, ballast, transformer) is **in scope**, because the output rating counts. |
| R3 — Multiple ratings | "For products with multiple voltage ratings, input or output, the products are considered within the scope of this Directive as soon as the highest of the ratings falls within the given voltage rating." | A 24 V AC device with a 230 V AC mains input is **in scope**. A device whose highest rating is 1 200 V AC is **outside** (above the band). |
| R4 — Above the band | Equipment exceeding 1 000 V AC or 1 500 V DC is outside the scope. | Do not assume "high voltage = LVD". Both the floor and the ceiling exclude. |
| R5 — AC and DC assessed separately | The band is expressed separately for AC and DC. | A 48 V DC rail is out (< 75 V DC) while a 48 V AC rail is out (< 50 V AC); a 60 V AC rail is in while a 60 V DC rail is out. |
| R6 — Annex II exclusions override | Even a product inside the band is excluded if it is listed in Annex II. | Not reached in this case: 24 V AC fails R1–R5 before any exclusion analysis. |
| R7 — Accessories and separate supplies | "Any accompanying battery-charger as well as equipment with integrated power supply unit within the voltage ranges of the Directive are in the scope of the LVD. This applies also, in the case of battery operated equipment with supply voltage rating below 50 V AC and 75 V DC, for their accompanying power supply unit." | The 24 V AC appliance is out; a **mains adapter shipped with it is separately in scope** and must carry its own LVD conformity assessment, CE marking and EU declaration of conformity. |

Annex II exclusions, listed for completeness (verify against the current consolidated text before relying on any one of them): explosive atmospheres; radiology and medical purposes; electrical parts of goods and passenger lifts; electricity meters; plugs and socket outlets for domestic use; electric fence controllers; radio-electrical interference; specialised equipment for ships, aircraft or railways complying with international safety provisions in which the Member States participate.

## 3. Application to the 24 V AC product — worked determination

**Declared rating to be used:** the nameplate / instruction-manual rating, not a bench measurement. If the product is marked "24 V AC ±10 %", the worst-case upper rating is 24 × 1.10 = 26.4 V AC — still below 50 V AC.

| Step | Test | Result for 24 V AC |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Is any rated input or output ≥ 50 V AC and ≤ 1 000 V AC? | No. Highest AC rating = 24 V AC (26.4 V AC at +10 %). 24 < 50. |
| 2 | Is any rated input or output ≥ 75 V DC and ≤ 1 500 V DC? | No. 24 < 75. |
| 3 | Is there any second rating (mains input, higher-voltage output, charger port) in either band? | Must be checked on the actual product; if yes → **in scope** (R2/R3). If no → out. |
| 4 | Annex II exclusion? | Not reached. |
| **Verdict** | | **Outside the scope of Directive 2014/35/EU**, provided step 3 is clean. |

**Conditions that flip the verdict to IN SCOPE** (all are about something other than the 24 V AC rail):

1. An integrated or built-in mains power supply — e.g. a 230 V AC / 24 V AC transformer or SMPS inside the enclosure. The product then has a rated input of 230 V AC, which is inside the band (R2/R3).
2. A rated output in the band — e.g. a 24 V AC input controller driving a 230 V AC contactor coil output that is a declared product rating, or a 24 V AC input inverter with a 230 V AC output.
3. A second model variant or a multi-voltage nameplate covering a mains rating. Variants are assessed on their own ratings; the family is in scope as soon as one rating is in the band.
4. The product is placed on the market as part of an assembly that itself carries a mains rating (e.g. a 24 V AC thermostat bundled into a 230 V AC control panel sold as one item).

**What does NOT flip the verdict:** internal step-up voltages, an internal 400 V bus, a flyback transformer secondary, an ignition coil, an ESD/impulse test level, or the presence of a 24 V AC SELV source. Per R1, internal voltages do not create scope.

**Caution on SELV reasoning:** 24 V AC is a classic SELV/extra-low-voltage control value, but do not use IEC 61140 SELV limits as the legal test. The LVD's DC floor (75 V) is deliberately lower than the 120 V DC ripple-free SELV limit, so a 100 V DC product can be SELV-compliant and still outside the LVD. The Directive's own numbers govern.

## 4. Consequences of being outside LVD scope

- No LVD conformity assessment, no LVD Annex III technical file obligation, no LVD EU declaration of conformity, and no CE marking *on LVD grounds*. A notified body is not involved.
- **The product still needs to be safe.** Absence of LVD scope is not a lowering of the safety bar; it changes which instrument carries the obligation.

**Instruments that likely still apply and must be assessed separately:**

| Instrument | Trigger | Note |
|---|---|---|
| EMC Directive 2014/30/EU | Almost certainly | No voltage threshold at all. Applies to apparatus liable to cause or be affected by electromagnetic disturbance. CE marking + EU DoC under EMC. |
| Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU | If any radio (Wi-Fi, BLE, LoRa, sub-GHz) | Article 3(1)(a) safety objective applies regardless of voltage. |
| General Product Safety Regulation (EU) 2023/988 | Consumer products, applicable from 13 Dec 2024 | Residual safety obligation, risk assessment, traceability, incident reporting. This is the main safety hook for out-of-LVD consumer goods. |
| Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC → Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 (applies 20 Jan 2027) | If the product is machinery or a safety component | Electrical hazards of machinery that *is* in LVD scope are covered by the LVD; for out-of-LVD machinery, machinery law carries it. |
| RoHS 2011/65/EU, REACH, Batteries Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 | Substance/battery content | Voltage-independent. |
| National law | Member State transpositions and general safety law | Out-of-LVD equipment remains subject to market surveillance under GPSR/national product safety law. |

**Recommended voluntary practice despite no legal obligation:** declare and test to the relevant product safety standard — EN IEC 60335-1 (appliances), EN IEC 62368-1 (AV/IT), EN 61010-1 (measurement, control, laboratory), EN 60730 (automatic controls), EN 61558-2-6 (safety isolating transformers). This gives a defensible safety position under GPSR, satisfies most OEM customers and insurers, and costs little if the design already targets those clearances. Keep the technical file and risk assessment regardless.

## 5. Boundary precision — quick reference

| Rated value | AC verdict | DC verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 24 V | Out (< 50) | Out (< 75) |
| 49.9 V | Out | Out |
| 50 V | **In** (lower bound inclusive) | Out |
| 75 V | In (if also ≥ 50 V AC on some rating) | **In** (lower bound inclusive) |
| 230 V / 400 V | In | In (≤ 1 500) |
| 1 000 V | **In** (upper bound inclusive) | In |
| 1 001 V AC | Out | In, if ≤ 1 500 V DC |
| 1 500 V DC | n/a | **In** |
| 1 501 V DC | n/a | Out |

**Bottom line:** the in-scope bands are 50–1 000 V AC and 75–1 500 V DC, rated input or output, both bounds inclusive; equipment designed for use at 24 V AC sits 26 V below the AC floor and is outside the scope of Directive 2014/35/EU, unless it also carries a rating inside either band (most commonly a 230 V AC mains input or a mains adapter supplied with it, the latter being separately in scope).

question: X8
answer:
# Compliance assessment — CRA reporting duty for an actively exploited vulnerability (awareness 17 November 2026)

**Instrument:** Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (Cyber Resilience Act), OJ L, 20.11.2024. Directly applicable; no national transposition required.

## 1. Bottom line

**Yes — the manufacturer must report now.** A product placed on the EU market in 2025 is inside the Article 14 reporting regime even though it is outside the CRA's substantive product requirements until 11 December 2027. The reporting obligations have applied since **11 September 2026**, and awareness on 17 November 2026 falls inside that window.

**Deadlines (Art. 14(2)), counted from awareness on 17 November 2026:**

| Stage | Legal rule | Trigger | Deadline on these facts |
|---|---|---|---|
| Early warning | Art. 14(2)(a) — without undue delay and in any event within **24 hours** of becoming aware | Awareness, 17 Nov 2026 | **18 November 2026** (same clock time) |
| Vulnerability notification | Art. 14(2)(b) — without undue delay and in any event within **72 hours** of becoming aware | Awareness, 17 Nov 2026 | **20 November 2026** |
| Final report | Art. 14(2)(c) — no later than **14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available** | Availability of the fix/mitigation, not awareness | Fix published 20 Nov 2026 → **4 December 2026**; fix already available at awareness → **1 December 2026** |

The final report date is **not** fixed at awareness; it floats with the remedy. The 24 h and 72 h clocks are calendar clocks — no business-day extension, no pause for internal investigation, no pause for the sensitivity flag.

## 2. Why the 2025 placing on the market does not defeat the duty

This is the point on which a superficially plausible 'no' rests, and it is wrong.

- **Art. 69(2)** provides that products placed on the market before 11 December 2027 are subject to the Regulation only if, from that date, they are subject to a substantial modification. On that provision alone, a 2025 product would escape.
- **Art. 69(3)** expressly derogates from Art. 69(2) so that **Article 14 applies to products with digital elements placed on the market before 11 December 2027**, whether or not they are ever modified. The Commission reaches the same conclusion in section 5.3 of its FAQs on CRA Implementation.
- Consequence: the product may never need CE marking under the CRA and may never need a conformity assessment, yet its installed base is fully in scope for reporting.

**Source quality flag:** the Art. 69(3) carve-out is decisive to this answer and is drawn from commentary citing Art. 69(2)-(3) and Commission FAQ §5.3 rather than from a verbatim OJ quotation in the research pack. Verify the exact wording of Art. 69(3) against the OJ before filing the assessment as final; the direction of the conclusion is not in doubt, but the citation should be pinned.

## 3. Scope gates (state these as conditions in the record)

1. **Product gate — Art. 3(1).** A connected consumer product (hardware with a network interface and/or its remote data processing solutions) is a 'product with digital elements'. Confirm no Art. 2(2)-(3) exclusion applies (medical devices under MDR/IVDR, motor vehicles, civil aviation, marine equipment, and the other listed sectoral regimes). If an exclusion applies, the CRA reporting duty falls away and the sectoral regime governs instead.
2. **Actor gate — Art. 3(13).** The duty-bearer is the manufacturer: the person who develops or manufactures the product, or has it designed/developed/manufactured, and markets it under its own name or trademark, whether sold, monetised or free of charge. Importers and distributors are **not** subject to the Art. 14 timelines; they must notify the manufacturer on becoming aware of a vulnerability.
3. **Temporal gate.** Awareness must fall on or after 11 September 2026 (Art. 71(2)). It does (17 Nov 2026).
4. **Product class is irrelevant here.** Art. 14 applies to all products with digital elements. Whether the product is 'important' (Annex III) or 'critical' (Annex IV) changes conformity-assessment route, not the reporting duty.

## 4. Trigger analysis — is this an 'actively exploited vulnerability'?

Art. 3(42): a vulnerability for which there is **reliable evidence that a malicious actor has demonstrably exploited it in a system without the permission of the owner**. The BSI Single Reporting Platform guidance adds the operative two-limb test: (i) the vulnerability is present in a product with digital elements; (ii) there is credible evidence of actual exploitation in real-world systems.

**Sufficient:** observed exploitation in the wild — telemetry, honeypot hits, incident reports from customers, CSIRT or CERT advisories reporting in-the-wild exploitation, vendor IR confirmation.

**Not sufficient on its own:** published exploit code, proof-of-concept code, port scans, a theoretical exploitability rating, a CVSS score, or inclusion in a vulnerability catalogue without exploitation evidence.

**Evidence to preserve now** (this is what makes the 24-hour filing defensible): the source and timestamp of the reliable information, the artefact showing real-world exploitation, the affected product and version identifiers, and the internal decision log recording when the manufacturer is treated as 'aware'. 'Awareness' should be documented as the point at which the manufacturer had sufficient information to conclude that an actively exploited vulnerability existed — not the point at which root-cause analysis completed.

## 5. Reporting channel and mechanics

- **Platform:** the CRA Single Reporting Platform (SRP), established under Art. 16 and operational since 11 September 2026. One submission; no parallel national filings.
- **Addressee:** the CSIRT designated as coordinator in the Member State where the manufacturer has its **main establishment** (Art. 14(7)) — in practice, where decisions about the products' cybersecurity are predominantly taken. If the manufacturer is not established in the EU, the coordinator follows the authorised representative.
- **ENISA:** the information is made available to ENISA simultaneously, save in exceptional circumstances.
- **Dissemination:** the receiving CSIRT shares the notification without delay with the CSIRTs of the Member States where the product has been made available. The early warning must therefore state those Member States where known (Art. 14(2)(a)).
- **Delayed dissemination:** the receiving CSIRT — not the manufacturer — may delay dissemination on justified cybersecurity grounds under Art. 16(2) and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/881 (adopted 11 December 2025).

**Correction of a false premise:** the CRA contains **no** 'knowingly and disproportionately exploited' withholding condition and no general exemption permitting a manufacturer to suppress or postpone a filing on proportionality, severity or reputational grounds. The only mechanism is the sensitivity marking plus the CSIRT's dissemination decision, and it does not move the filing deadline. Anyone advising that a filing can be deferred on those grounds is applying NIS2-style or pre-CRA reasoning that is not in the text.

**Second false premise:** the vulnerability track has **no severity threshold**. 'Severe' is a term of art for the separate incident track (Art. 3(44), Art. 14(5)). A low-CVSS actively exploited vulnerability is reportable.

**No MSME carve-out.** There is no microenterprise or SME exemption from Art. 14. The CRA's MSME relief concerns fees and administrative simplification, not the reporting trigger. Confirm against Commission guidance §9.1 and the Commission FAQs §5.

## 6. Content required at each stage

**24-hour early warning (Art. 14(2)(a)) — deliberately thin.** Mandatory fields per ENISA's published data set: notification type and level; manufacturer name; the product; a title; the Member States where the product has been made available. Substantive analysis is not due at 24 hours. For an incident-track filing, add whether unlawful or malicious acts are suspected.

**72-hour vulnerability notification (Art. 14(2)(b)).** General information as available on: the product concerned; the general nature of the exploit; the general nature of the vulnerability; corrective or mitigating measures already taken; corrective or mitigating measures users can take; and the manufacturer's assessment of the sensitivity of the information. The clause 'unless the relevant information has already been provided' prevents duplication — it does not permit skipping the 72-hour stage by over-loading the 24-hour warning.

**Final report (Art. 14(2)(c)) — due 14 days after the remedy is available.** Must include: a full description of the vulnerability and its exploitation; severity and impact; an initial assessment; details of the attacker where known; details of the security update or other protective measures; and the date on which the remedy became available.

**Practical sequencing note.** Reports may be updated through the SRP until the final report is submitted; after that, editing is generally closed. Do not hold the 24-hour warning back to improve it — file thin and update.

**Interpretive point to confirm with the coordinating CSIRT.** If the corrective measure was already available before awareness (e.g. the patch shipped before exploitation came to light), a literal reading of Art. 14(2)(c) would produce a deadline that expired before the manufacturer knew anything. The defensible position is that the 14-day period cannot run before awareness, so the deadline is 14 days from the later of awareness and remedy availability — here **1 December 2026**. Record that reasoning in the filing rather than letting the date pass silently.

## 7. The parallel incident track — do not conflate it

If the exploitation also meets the severe-incident test (Art. 3(44), Art. 14(5) — e.g. it negatively affects or is capable of negatively affecting the product's ability to protect availability, authenticity, integrity or confidentiality of data or functions, or has led or is capable of leading to the introduction or execution of malicious code), a second notification track is triggered:

| Stage | Vulnerability track (Art. 14(2)) | Severe-incident track (Art. 14(3)-(4)) |
|---|---|---|
| Early warning | 24 hours | 24 hours |
| Second notification | 72 hours (vulnerability notification) | 72 hours (incident notification) |
| Final report | **14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available** | **1 month after the 72-hour incident notification** (→ 20 December 2026 on these facts) |

The two 24-hour and 72-hour deadlines coincide, so a single SRP submission can carry both where the fields overlap. The final-report deadlines diverge; calendar both. Where a severe incident is in play, the later date governs the last filing but the earlier date is the safe operating deadline.

## 8. Cumulative obligations

Art. 14 reporting does not displace other regimes. Run in parallel:

- **NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555), Art. 23** — if the manufacturer is itself an essential or important entity, the 24-hour early warning / 72-hour incident notification / one-month final report run separately to the CSIRT or competent authority. Art. 14 does not substitute for it. Verify whether a national convergence mechanism applies in the relevant Member State.
- **GDPR, Art. 33-34** — if personal data is affected, 72-hour notification to the supervisory authority and, where the threshold is met, communication to data subjects.
- **Sectoral regimes** — if the product is in a regulated vertical (medical, automotive, aviation), those authorities may also require notification; if an Art. 2 exclusion applies, that regime replaces the CRA entirely.
- **Contractual and customer notification** — separate from Art. 14, manufacturers must provide security updates and disseminate information about fixed vulnerabilities and user-facing mitigations (Art. 13 and Annex I, Part II). Users must be told what to do; that is not optional and is not satisfied by the regulatory filing alone.

## 9. Consequences of getting it wrong

Member States must lay down penalties for infringement of the manufacturer obligations, including Art. 14 (Art. 64). The top tier — **up to EUR 15 million or 2.5% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher** — is the figure to plan against for infringement of the Annex I requirements and the Chapter II manufacturer obligations; confirm the precise tiering against Art. 64(3)-(5) before relying on it in a board paper. Beyond fines: market surveillance authority measures, corrective-action orders, withdrawal or recall, and the loss of the reporting record that would otherwise evidence diligence in any later product-liability or negligence claim.

## 10. Immediate action plan (day 0 = 17 November 2026)

1. **Freeze the awareness timestamp.** Record who knew what, when, and on what evidence. This fixes all three clocks.
2. **Classify.** Confirm the product is a product with digital elements and not in an Art. 2 exclusion; confirm manufacturer status; record whether the severe-incident limbs are also met.
3. **Identify the coordinating CSIRT** by main establishment (Art. 14(7)); confirm SRP account and credentials are live.
4. **File the early warning by 18 November 2026** with: notification type/level, manufacturer name, product, title, Member States of availability. Do not wait for root cause.
5. **Prepare the vulnerability notification for 20 November 2026** covering product, nature of the exploit and vulnerability, measures taken, user mitigations, sensitivity assessment.
6. **Set the final-report clock on remedy availability.** Target a fix or documented mitigation; on release, the final report is due 14 days later (4 December 2026 if released 20 November 2026).
7. **Issue user-facing guidance** on mitigations independently of the regulatory filing.
8. **Check NIS2 and GDPR** triggers the same day; diarise those deadlines separately.
9. **Log the sensitivity marking** and any request that the CSIRT withhold onward dissemination under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/881 — as a request, not as a delay to filing.

## 11. Conditions that would change this answer

- The product falls within an Art. 2(2)-(3) exclusion → CRA reporting duty does not apply; the sectoral regime governs.
- The reporting party is an importer or distributor only → no Art. 14 timelines; duty is to notify the manufacturer.
- The information available amounts only to published exploit code, a PoC or scanning activity, with no reliable evidence of real-world exploitation → Art. 3(42) is not met, and no filing is due (monitor and document the assessment).
- Awareness pre-dates 11 September 2026 and nothing new was learned after that date → the Art. 14 duty is not engaged for that pre-existing knowledge; confirm against the Commission FAQ on pre-September 2026 knowledge.
- Art. 69(3) does not in fact read as the commentary reports → the 2025 product would fall outside Art. 14 and the answer flips to 'no'. This is the single highest-value verification item and should be closed before the assessment is signed off.

question: X11
shape: UN vehicle regulation (electric power train, UN R100)
answer:
# Minimum isolation resistance, HV bus to electrical chassis — combined (galvanically connected) AC/DC 400 V system, UN R100 05 series (OJ L, 17.8.2026, Reg. (EU) 2026/1695)

## 0. Answer

| Case | Governing criterion | Working voltage U | R_min = criterion x U | R_min (kΩ) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **(a)** Combined AC/DC train, AC buses with none of the extra protections | **500 Ω/V** | 400 V | 500 x 400 = 200 000 Ω | **200 kΩ** |
| **(b)** Combined AC/DC train, **all** AC HV buses protected by one of the two measures in 5.1.3.2(a)/(b) | **100 Ω/V** | 400 V | 100 x 400 = 40 000 Ω | **40 kΩ** |

Scaling for other working voltages, for reference: R_min[kΩ] = 0.5 x U[V] unprotected, R_min[kΩ] = 0.1 x U[V] protected.

## 1. Which clause governs, and why

The premise "galvanically connected AC and DC buses" selects **paragraph 5.1.3.2 (Electric power train consisting of combined DC- and AC-buses)**. Paragraph 5.1.3.1 (separate DC/AC buses: 100 Ω/V for DC buses, 500 Ω/V for AC buses) does not apply to this vehicle, because it is conditioned on the AC and DC buses being galvanically isolated from each other.

Operative text of 5.1.3.2 (EN, OJ L 17.8.2026):

> "If AC high voltage buses and DC high voltage buses are galvanically connected, isolation resistance between the high voltage bus and the electrical chassis shall have a minimum value of 500 Ω/volt of the working voltage.
>
> However, if all AC high voltage buses are protected by one of the two following measures, isolation resistance between the high voltage bus and the electrical chassis shall have a minimum value of 100 Ω/V of the working voltage:
> (a) …"

Three consequences that drive the answer:

1. **Default is 500 Ω/V**, applied to the *combined* high-voltage bus (the requirement is written once, against "the high voltage bus", not per bus type). This is case (a).
2. **The 100 Ω/V relaxation is conditional on "all" AC high-voltage buses** being protected by *one of* the two listed measures. "All" is a hard, whole-system condition: a single unprotected AC HV segment anywhere in the vehicle (e.g. an AC compressor or AC PTC heater whose terminals are not double-protected) removes the relaxation for the entire combined bus and returns the requirement to 500 Ω/V.
3. The relaxation is *one of* the two measures — either alone is sufficient; they are not cumulative.

### The two measures (5.1.3.2)

- **(a)** At least two or more layers of solid insulators, protective barriers or enclosures that independently provide protection against direct contact (i.e. meeting the direct-contact provisions of 5.1.1.1 / 5.1.1.2). This is quoted verbatim in the retrieved OJ text.
- **(b)** The second alternative enumerated in 5.1.3.2(b). The retrieved passage truncates at the start of item (a), so the exact wording of (b) is not reproduced here rather than being paraphrased from memory. **This does not affect either numeric answer**, because the criterion is 100 Ω/V under *either* measure.

## 2. Calculation, with units carried through

The Regulation states the criterion in **Ω per volt of working voltage**. With U = 400 V:

**Case (a) — no AC protections:**

    R_min = 500 Ω/V x 400 V = 200 000 Ω
    R_min = 200 000 Ω / 1000 Ω/kΩ = 200 kΩ

**Case (b) — all AC buses protected by measure (a) or (b):**

    R_min = 100 Ω/V x 400 V = 40 000 Ω
    R_min = 40 000 Ω / 1000 Ω/kΩ = 40 kΩ

The 400 V is used directly as the working voltage; no conversion is applied. Per the Regulation, working voltage for an AC bus is its RMS value, so a 400 V RMS AC bus and a 400 V DC bus in a galvanically connected train give a single working voltage of 400 V for the combined bus. If the working voltage were declared differently (e.g. a boosted section at a higher voltage), the criterion scales linearly and the values above scale with it.

## 3. Internal consistency checks

**3.1 Against the Annex 7A test-resistor bounds (these must bracket the stated minima).**

Annex 7A requires the verification resistor Ro to be sized so that:

- when the applicable minimum is **100 Ω/V**: `1/(1/(95U) - 1/Ri) ≤ Ro < 1/(1/(100U) - 1/Ri)`
- when the applicable minimum is **500 Ω/V**: `1/(1/(475U) - 1/Ri) ≤ Ro < 1/(1/(500U) - 1/Ri)`

At U = 400 V:

| Applicable minimum | 95 %-of-criterion x U | criterion x U | Stated R_min | Consistent? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 Ω/V (case b) | 38 000 Ω | 40 000 Ω | 40 kΩ | yes — 40 kΩ is the 100U bound |
| 500 Ω/V (case a) | 190 000 Ω | 200 000 Ω | 200 kΩ | yes — 200 kΩ is the 500U bound |

The 95 %/100 % and 475 %/500 % brackets in the Regulation sit exactly around the two numbers reported, confirming the criterion-to-kΩ conversion is the one the Regulation itself uses.

**3.2 Against the separate-bus clause (sanity check on interpretation).**

Under 5.1.3.1 (buses isolated from each other) the same 400 V system would need 100 Ω/V x 400 V = 40 kΩ for the DC bus and 500 Ω/V x 400 V = 200 kΩ for the AC bus. The combined-bus rule in 5.1.3.2 is therefore exactly: *if the AC bus is fully touch-protected, the whole train may be assessed at the DC-level criterion; if not, the whole train is assessed at the AC-level criterion.* That is precisely what cases (a) and (b) capture, and it explains the 5x ratio between the two answers.

**3.3 Ordering check.** 200 kΩ (a) > 40 kΩ (b). The unprotected configuration is the binding requirement; a design that demonstrates 200 kΩ automatically satisfies 40 kΩ. No value stated in this deliverable violates a threshold it sets.

**3.4 Measurement-condition check (Annex 5A).** The isolation resistance is measured with a DC instrument applying at least half the working voltage — for this vehicle, **≥ 200 V DC** between live parts and chassis — and Ri is computed from the U1/U2 voltage readings with a known Ro, then divided by the working voltage to give Ω/V. The test voltage (200 V) is a test condition and is independent of the 200 kΩ / 40 kΩ limits; there is no interaction between them.

## 4. What this means for the design and for the isolation monitor

- **Design target.** The regulatory values are compliance floors, not design targets. Vehicle isolation resistance falls with humidity, coolant ingress, Y-capacitor/EMI-filter leakage and ageing. Set the end-of-life design target at roughly 2x the applicable floor — **≥ 400 kΩ** if the vehicle relies on case (a), or **≥ 80 kΩ** if it qualifies for case (b). (These margins are engineering recommendations, not Regulation values.)
- **Monitor thresholds.** The on-board isolation monitoring system must warn before the bus falls below the *applicable* floor (200 kΩ or 40 kΩ), and the applicable floor must be fixed at type-approval time by the protection status of the AC buses — not switched at runtime.
- **Where the 100 Ω/V relaxation is won or lost.** Any AC high-voltage node — traction inverter AC output feeding the compressor, AC PTC heater, AC charging path if the on-board charger presents an AC HV bus — must be enclosed by the two-layer / barrier / enclosure protection of measure (a) (or by measure (b)). One unqualified AC node moves the whole vehicle to 200 kΩ, i.e. it multiplies the required isolation by five. Treat the protection status of every AC node as a configuration-controlled item in the BOM and harness drawings.
- **Documentation for type approval.** Record, per AC HV node, which measure (5.1.3.2(a) or (b)) is applied, with the corresponding drawing/section reference; the approval authority will use those drawings to confirm that isolation resistance between live parts and chassis is unaffected by the protection.

## 5. Verification items (open points, none of which change the two numbers)

1. Confirm the exact wording of 5.1.3.2(b) against the OJ text — it was truncated in the retrieved passage and is described above only as the second enumerated alternative.
2. Confirm the declared "working voltage" of the combined train is 400 V under the Regulation's definition (highest voltage between live parts; RMS for AC) and that no section of the train (e.g. a boost-converter rail) carries a higher working voltage that would raise the required resistance proportionally.
3. Confirm the vehicle is type-approved to the 05 series of amendments as published in OJ L, 17.8.2026 (Reg. (EU) 2026/1695) and not to an earlier or later series; the 5.1.3.2 structure and the 500/100 Ω/V values above are read from that text.
