The answer gives 40 kΩ for ask 2, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: X14
shape: EU radio equipment (RED cybersecurity delegated act)
answer:
DETERMINATION — Bluetooth-connected insulin pump (medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745) and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30

== 1. ANSWERS ==

(1) Do the cybersecurity essential requirements of Article 3(3), points (d), (e) and (f), of Directive 2014/53/EU, as specified by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30, apply to the pump? — NO. They are expressly disapplied. Article 2(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 provides: 'By way of derogation from Article 1, the essential requirements set out in Article 3(3), points (d), (e) and (f), of Directive 2014/53/EU shall not apply to radio equipment to which either of the following Union legislation also applies: (a) Regulation (EU) 2017/745; (b) Regulation (EU) 2017/746.' The pump is radio equipment to which Regulation (EU) 2017/745 also applies, so Article 2(1)(a) removes all three requirements from it.

(2) Date from which Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 applies to the radio equipment it does cover? — 1 AUGUST 2025. Article 3, second paragraph, of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30, as replaced by Article 1 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2444 of 20 July 2023: 'It shall apply from 1 August 2025.' (The original second paragraph read 'It shall apply from 1 August 2024'; that date was superseded by the 2023 amendment, which entered into force on its publication in the Official Journal on 27 October 2023 and is reflected in the consolidated text of 27/10/2023.)

== 2. LEGAL CHAIN ==

Step 1 — Is the pump radio equipment within Directive 2014/53/EU?
Yes. Bluetooth communication is radio communication, so the pump meets the Article 2 definition of radio equipment. The exclusions in Article 1(2) and 1(3) and in Annex I of the Directive (amateur radio, marine equipment, airborne products, custom R&D evaluation kits; public security/defence/State security) do not cover medical devices. Being a medical device does not remove a product from the RED; the two regimes apply cumulatively. Recital (8) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 confirms the point: 'Directive 2014/53/EU applies to products that meet the definition of "radio equipment" ... no requirements of Directive 2014/53/EU make a distinction between the radio and non-radio functions of the radio equipment and therefore all aspects and parts of the equipment should comply with the essential requirements provided for in this delegated regulation.'

Step 2 — Would the pump fall in a covered category under Article 1 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 but for the derogation?
Probably yes, at least for points (d) and (e), if the pump reaches the internet through a paired smartphone app or gateway: Article 1(1) captures 'any radio equipment that can communicate itself over the internet, whether it communicates directly or via any other equipment ("internet-connected radio equipment")', and Article 1(2)(a) applies point (e) to internet-connected radio equipment that processes personal data (an insulin pump processes health data, i.e. special-category personal data under Article 9 GDPR, and traffic/location data). Point (f) (transfer of money, monetary value or virtual currency) would not be engaged by a pump. This step is recorded for completeness only: it is superseded by Step 3 and is not the basis of the answer. Note: point (d) of Article 1(2) is not reproduced in the source text retrieved and is not relied on here.

Step 3 — The controlling provision: Article 2(1) derogation.
Because Regulation (EU) 2017/745 applies to the pump, Article 2(1)(a) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 disapplies Article 3(3)(d), (e) and (f) of the RED in respect of it. The derogation is automatic and objective — it is not an election by the manufacturer, and it is not limited to particular device classes. Its consequence is that the three cybersecurity essential requirements are not essential requirements for this product at all, so no presumption-of-conformity route, notified-body assessment or declaration-of-conformity reference under those points is required or appropriate.

Conclusion: the answer to the first ask is NO.

== 3. WHAT STILL APPLIES TO THE PUMP ==

- Directive 2014/53/EU continues to apply in full except for Article 3(3)(d), (e) and (f): Article 3(1)(a) (protection of health and safety), Article 3(1)(b) (adequate level of electromagnetic compatibility) and Article 3(2) (effective and efficient use of the radio spectrum) remain essential requirements, with the corresponding conformity assessment under Article 17 and the RED technical documentation.
- The device carries a single CE marking covering both instruments; the EU declaration of conformity must reference Directive 2014/53/EU and Regulation (EU) 2017/745, and the RED technical file must record why Article 3(3)(d), (e) and (f) are not applicable (Article 2(1)(a) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30).
- Cybersecurity obligations for the pump arise under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 instead: Annex I general safety and performance requirements for devices incorporating electronic programmable systems (software lifecycle, state-of-the-art IT security, protection against unauthorised access, minimum IT requirements for the operating environment) and for the interaction of software with the device's characteristics, together with the manufacturer's post-market surveillance and vigilance duties. Verify the current MDR Annex I point numbering and current MDCG guidance on medical device cybersecurity before finalising the technical documentation, as those references were not part of the retrieved corpus.

== 4. BOUNDARY CONDITIONS ON THIS DETERMINATION ==

- The determination rests on Regulation (EU) 2017/745 applying to the product as placed on the market. If a radio item is placed on the market separately from the MDR device (e.g. a standalone Bluetooth module or a non-medical companion hub or consumer accessory sold as a spare part in its own right), that item is radio equipment to which the MDR does not apply, the Article 2(1) derogation is unavailable for it, and the Article 1 scoping test must be run for it separately — with compliance required from 1 August 2025.
- The converse also holds: the derogation cannot be claimed for equipment that is not in fact covered by the MDR (e.g. a wellness-only accessory).
- Should the Commission amend Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 to alter the Article 2(1) derogation, this determination must be revisited. No such amendment was found in the sources consulted; the position stated reflects the consolidated text of 27/10/2023.

== 5. DOCUMENTATION ACTION (one paragraph for the RED technical file) ==

'Article 3(3), points (d), (e) and (f), of Directive 2014/53/EU are not applicable to this radio equipment. The equipment is a medical device to which Regulation (EU) 2017/745 applies; accordingly, pursuant to Article 2(1)(a) of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30, the essential requirements set out in those points do not apply to it. The cybersecurity of the device is addressed under Regulation (EU) 2017/745, Annex I, and is documented in the medical device technical documentation. The remaining essential requirements of Article 3(1)(a), 3(1)(b) and 3(2) of Directive 2014/53/EU are complied with as demonstrated in this technical file.'

== 6. SOURCES RELIED ON ==

- Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 (OJ L 7, 12.1.2022, p. 6; consolidated version 27/10/2023) — Articles 1, 2, 3 and recital (8): https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2022/30/oj/eng and https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32022R0030
- Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2444 of 20 July 2023 (OJ L, 2023/2444, 27.10.2023) — Articles 1 and 3: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=OJ:L_202302444
- Directive 2014/53/EU — Articles 1, 2, 3, Annex I: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32014L0053

FIPS 197 (Advanced Encryption Standard), AES-256 — parameter report

Scope: raw AES-256 block cipher as specified in FIPS 197 (FIPS PUB 197, 2001; updated 2023 with no technical changes to the algorithm). No mode of operation is involved.

1. Number of rounds: 14.
Basis: FIPS 197 Figure 4 (Key-Block-Round Combinations) lists AES-256 as Nk = 8 words, Nb = 4 words, Nr = 14. Section 5 states Nr = 14 when Nk = 8. The cipher therefore executes 14 iterations of the round function, with an initial AddRoundKey before round 1 and a final round that omits MixColumns.

2. Block size: 128 bits.
Basis: FIPS 197 Section 3.1 states that the input and output each consist of sequences of 128 bits. Section 5 states that the length of the input block, the output block, and the State is 128 bits, represented by Nb = 4 32-bit words. This block size is fixed for AES-128, AES-192, and AES-256.

3. Number of round keys consumed: 15 round keys, each an array of four words.
Derivation: FIPS 197 Section 5.2 (Key Expansion) generates Nb(Nr + 1) words. For AES-256: 4 x (14 + 1) = 60 words. Each round key consists of Nb = 4 words (Section 5.1.4, AddRoundKey), so 60 / 4 = 15 round keys. Equivalently, the cipher applies AddRoundKey once before the round loop and once in each of the 14 rounds: 1 + 14 = 15 applications, each consuming one four-word round key.
Indexing: round key 0 = w[0..3], round key 1 = w[4..7], ..., round key 14 = w[56..59]. The expanded key is 60 words = 1920 bits = 240 bytes; the first Nk = 8 words are the AES-256 cipher key and the remaining 52 words are generated by the key schedule.

Consistency check:
- Rounds: 14.
- Round keys: Nr + 1 = 15; 15 x 4 words = 60 words; 60 x 32 bits = 1920 bits.
- Total round-key bits formula: block length x (rounds + 1) = 128 x 15 = 1920 bits.
These agree: 14 rounds, 128-bit block, 15 four-word round keys.

Summary answer:
AES-256 uses 14 rounds, has a 128-bit block size, and consumes 15 round keys, each a four-word (128-bit) array.

Citations: FIPS 197, Figure 4; Sections 3.1, 5, 5.1.4, and 5.2.

ANSWERS (NIST SP 800-171, Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Nonfederal Systems and Organizations)

2. COUNTING CONVENTION (stated so the numbers are reproducible)

The 14 families above, plus three added in Rev. 3:

# Default multiprocessing start method on Linux — CPython 3.15 documentation

## 1. Answers

| # | Question | Answer (3.15 docs) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Default start method on Linux when `set_start_method()` is never called | **`forkserver`** — except when there is no writable temporary directory, in which case **`spawn`** |
| 2 | Linux default before Python 3.14 | **`fork`** |
| 3 | Condition under which the default becomes `spawn` | **When there is no writable temporary directory** (`tempfile.gettempdir()`), which the fork server requires — e.g. a read-only file system |

Scope note: the documentation does not single out “Linux” in the default-method sentences; it says **POSIX**, and describes `forkserver` as available on “POSIX platforms which support passing file descriptors over Unix pipes **such as Linux**”. Linux is therefore an instance of the class the default is stated for, and the answer above is the Linux answer.

## 2. Ask 1 — the current (3.15) Linux default is `forkserver`

From the 3.15 `multiprocessing` page, the `forkserver` entry in *Contexts and start methods* (verbatim, line wraps from the page):

> “`forkserver`
> When the program starts and selects the forkserver start method, a server process is spawned. …
> Available on POSIX platforms which support passing file descriptors over Unix pipes such as Linux.  **The default on those, unless there is no writable temporary directory (see `tempfile.gettempdir()`), which the fork server requires; spawn is the default in that case.**
> Changed in version 3.14: This became the default start method on POSIX platforms.”

So, with the default determined normally (a writable tempdir exists), a Linux program that never calls `set_start_method()` gets **`forkserver`**. This is confirmed independently by the closing sentence of the same section's change log:

> “Changed in version 3.14: On POSIX platforms the default start method was changed from fork to forkserver.”

Mechanism (worth stating because it explains “never calls `set_start_method()`”):

- `multiprocessing.get_start_method(allow_none=False)` — “If the global start method is not set and *allow_none* is `False`, the global start method is set to the default, and its name is returned.”
- `multiprocessing.get_context(method=Noun)` — “if the global start method has not been set, this will set it to the system default”.
- Many primitives (`Lock`, `RLock`, `Semaphore`, `BoundedSemaphore`, `Condition`, `Event`, `Queue`, `Pool`, `Process`, …) are documented as “Instantiating this class may set the global start method.”
- Since **3.15.1** the default is “determined when it is first needed rather than when `multiprocessing` is imported” (gh-155717). Importing the module alone therefore tells you nothing; the value is fixed at first use.
- `get_all_start_methods()` “Returns a list of the supported start methods, **the first of which is the default**” — a documented mechanism, though the 3.15 page does not print the per-platform list order in the passages consulted, so do not rely on the literal ordering without checking on the box.

Contrast (not the Linux answer, listed to keep the platform split explicit):

- **macOS:** `spawn` is the default since 3.8 (“The `fork` start method should be considered unsafe as it can lead to crashes of the subprocess…”, bpo-33725).
- **Windows:** only `spawn` is available; child processes no longer inherit all inheritable handles (3.4).

## 3. Ask 2 — before 3.14 the Linux/POSIX default was `fork`

The same `versionchanged:: 3.14` note is the direct evidence: the POSIX default “was changed **from `fork`** to `forkserver`”. Therefore, in every documented release before 3.14 (i.e. 3.13 and earlier, on POSIX/Linux where `fork` is available), the default was **`fork`**. Two qualifications the docs supply:

- `fork` remains *available* on Linux after 3.14 — it stopped being the default, it was not removed. The available set on Linux is `forkserver`, `fork`, `spawn`.
- `forkserver` itself dates from 3.4 (“`spawn` added on all POSIX platforms, and `forkserver` added for some POSIX platforms”), but it only became the default in 3.14.

## 4. Ask 3 — when the default becomes `spawn`

Condition, exactly as documented (3.15 page, `forkserver` entry):

> “The default on those, **unless there is no writable temporary directory (see `tempfile.gettempdir()`), which the fork server requires; spawn is the default in that case.**”

And the change note on the 3.15 page:

> “Changed in version **3.15.1**: `spawn` is now the default start method when there is no writable temporary directory, **for example on a read-only file system**. Previously `forkserver` remained the default there and starting a process failed with an `OSError`. The default is determined when it is first needed rather than when `multiprocessing` is imported. See gh-155717.”

So the trigger is **environmental, not a code path**: the writability of `tempfile.gettempdir()` (in practice, the directory named by `TMPDIR`/`TEMP`/`TMP` if set, else `/tmp`), evaluated at first need. If it is not writable — read-only root file system, a container with `/tmp` mounted read-only, a sandboxed CI runner, etc. — `spawn` is the default and no `OSError` is raised for the forkserver setup.

Version-label caveat (so no reader thinks the sources disagree): the identical gh-155717 change is rendered as **3.15.1** on the 3.15 page, **3.14.9** on the 3.14 page, and **3.16** on the dev/3.16 page — one change, backported to each maintenance branch. For the 3.15 series the correct label is **3.15.1**; a 3.15.**0** doc snapshot would still say `forkserver` remained the default there and that process start failed with `OSError`.

## 5. Verification recipe (optional; the answer is a documentation fact, not a measurement)

```bash
# Normal Linux, writable tempdir -> forkserver
python3.15 -c 'import multiprocessing as mp; print(mp.get_start_method())'
# expected: forkserver

# No writable temporary directory -> spawn (3.15.1+)
TMPDIR=/proc python3.15 -c 'import multiprocessing as mp; print(mp.get_start_method())'
# expected: spawn   (on 3.15.0 / 3.14.8 this instead raised OSError when starting a process)
```

Pitfalls when checking: (a) call `get_start_method()` **before** constructing any `Lock`/`Queue`/`Pool`/`Process`, because instantiating them may fix the global method; (b) `get_start_method(allow_none=True)` returns `Nou` instead of fixing the default; (c) `set_start_method(..., force=True)` anywhere in sitecustomize/`usercustomize` will defeat the test; (d) do not test the tempdir case with a *nonexistent* path alone — `tempfile.gettempdir()` falls back, so use a genuinely read-only mount or `/proc`.

## 6. Provenance of the quoted sources

| Source | sha256 (prefix) | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `https://docs.python.org/3.15/library/multiprocessing.html` | `0a06c38e4a4e` | Primary — asks 1, 2, 3 |
| `https://github.com/python/cpythone/blob/v3.14.8/Doc/library/multiprocessing.rst` | `e059fc9611ce` | Cross-check of the `versionchanged:: 3.14` note and `set_start_method` semantics |
| `https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/multiprocessing.html` | `6049c3f0ef6e` | Confirms same wording; labels the tempdir change **3.14.9** |
| `https://docs.python.org/3.16/library/multiprocessing.html` and `https://docs.python.org/uk/dev/library/multiprocessing.html` | `4384299d366b`, `fe624c95aa5a` | Confirms the change is labelled **3.16** on the development branch (same gh-155717) |
| `https://docs.python.org/3/library/multiprocessing.html?highlight=queue` | `0a06c38e4a4e` | Identical hash to the 3.15 page — the unversioned `/3/` URL currently serves the same text |

## 7. Residual uncertainties (documentation-role caveats)

1. **Snapshot, not a release guarantee.** The 3.15 page fetched is the living documentation for the 3.15 series; the tempdir rule appears only from 3.15.1. If the intended target is 3.15.0 exactly, ask 3 has no documented trigger and ask 1 is unconditionally `forkserver`.
2. **“Linux” vs “POSIX”.** The default is stated for POSIX; Linux qualifies as a POSIX platform that passes file descriptors over Unix pipes. A POSIX platform *without* that capability would not have `forkserver` at all and would fall back to `fork`; that is not Linux.
3. **Documented default vs runtime behavior.** Everything above is what the documentation states. The runtime value can be overridden by `set_start_method()`, by `get_context(...)`, or by `multiprocessing` being configured in a startup hook — the question explicitly excludes that case.
4. **`get_all_start_methods()` ordering.** The docs assert “the first of which is the default” but the consulted passages do not enumerate the Linux ordering; do not quote a literal list order from this document.

## 8. One-line answer

On Linux in the CPython 3.15 documentation, a program that never calls `set_start_method()` gets **`forkserver`** (it was **`fork`** before 3.14), and the default becomes **`spawn`** only when there is no writable temporary directory for the fork server to use — e.g. a read-only file system (documented as a 3.15.1 change).

WebAssembly 3.0 core specification — memory page size and declared-page maxima (i32 / i64)

1. ANSWERS

| # | Question | Value | Unit | Equivalent |
|---|----------|-------|------|------------|
| 1 | Page size | 65,536 | bytes | 2^16 B = 64 KiB |
| 2 | Max pages a memory may declare, address type i32 | 65,536 | pages | 2^16 pages |
| 3 | That maximum in bytes | 4,294,967,296 | bytes | 2^32 B = 4 GiB |
| 4 | Corresponding page limit, address type i64 | 281,474,976,710,656 | pages | 2^48 pages = 2^64 B = 16 EiB |

2. WHERE EACH NUMBER COMES FROM (core spec, not an embedding)

2.1 Page size — 65,536 bytes.
The spec defines linear-memory size as a count of pages, with the page size a fixed constant of 65,536 (2^16) bytes. It is a spec constant, not a host/OS page size and not implementation-defined. Every memory size in the spec (memory.size, memory.grow, limits, the runtime memory instance size) is expressed in these units.

2.2 Limits and their range k.
A memory type is `at lim`, where `at` is the address type (i32 or i64) and `lim` is a limits pair {min n, max m}. Validation of a limits pair is parameterised by a range k:
  - {min n, max ε} is valid within range k  iff  n ≤ k
  - {min n, max m} is valid within range k  iff  n ≤ m ≤ k
The memory type is valid iff its limits are valid within range k, where
  k = 2^16  when at = i32
  k = 2^48  when at = i64
Because limits are page counts, k is in pages. Therefore the largest number that may appear in either the min or the max field of a declared memory is 2^16 pages for i32 and 2^48 pages for i64. A module whose declared min or max exceeds k is invalid and must be rejected at validation (CompileError in the JS embedding).

2.3 Binary encoding (why the two address types differ in width, not in unit).
The limits form carries an address-type flag; page counts stay page-granular in both cases, but the field width changes:
  0x00 n:u32        ⇒ i32, {min n, max ε}
  0x01 n:u32 m:u32  ⇒ i32, {min n, max m}
  0x02 n:u32        ⇒ i32, {min n, max ε}, shared (threads)
  0x03 n:u32 m:u32  ⇒ i32, {min n, max m}, shared (threads)
  0x04 n:u64        ⇒ i64, {min n, max ε}
  0x05 n:u64 m:u64  ⇒ i64, {min n, max m}
  0x06 n:u64        ⇒ i64, {min n, max ε}, shared (threads)
  0x07 n:u64 m:u64  ⇒ i64, {min n, max m}, shared (threads)
Consequence: 2^16 pages fits a u32 field; 2^48 pages does not (2^48 > 2^32-1) and requires the u64 encoding 0x04–0x07. A decoder that reads an i64 memory's limits as u32, or that caps an i64 memory at 2^16 pages, is wrong.

3. ARITHMETIC VERIFICATION (all numbers above cross-checked)

- Page size: 2^16 = 65,536 bytes.
- i32 byte maximum: 65,536 pages × 65,536 bytes/page = 2^16 × 2^16 = 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 bytes. Independent check: 65536 × 65536 = 4,294,967,296. Equals 4 GiB (gibibytes, not 4 × 10^9 bytes).
- i64 page maximum: 2^48 = 281,474,976,710,656 pages. Encodable in u64 (max 18,446,744,073,709,551,615).
- i64 byte maximum: 2^48 pages × 2^16 bytes/page = 2^64 = 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 bytes = 16 EiB.
- Address-space symmetry (the decisive check):
    i32: 2^16 pages ↔ 2^32 bytes ↔ i32 address space 0..2^32-1  → exact fit.
    i64: 2^48 pages ↔ 2^64 bytes ↔ i64 address space 0..2^64-1  → exact fit.
  Both maxima fill their address space exactly, with the top byte at offset (space size − 1). One page more (2^16+1 or 2^48+1) would exceed the addressable range; hence these are the correct tight upper bounds, not approximations.
- Ordering check against embedding limits (see §4): 2^48 pages > 2^37−1 pages > 2^18 pages, i.e. core i64 limit > JS API declarable limit > JS API runtime size cap. Monotonic, no contradiction.

4. SCOPE NOTE — CORE SPEC vs EMBEDDING (do not conflate these numbers)

The values in §1 are the core specification's limits. The WebAssembly JS API embedding (a separate document) imposes stricter, implementation-level limits, which are frequently misquoted as the core answer:

| Level | 32-bit memory | 64-bit memory |
|-------|---------------|---------------|
| Core spec — max min/max field (validation) | 65,536 pages (4 GiB) | 2^48 pages (2^64 B = 16 EiB) |
| JS API — max min/max field (compile-time) | 65,536 pages (4 GiB) | 2^37−1 pages (2^53−2^16 B ≈ 8 PiB) |
| JS API — max runtime size | 65,536 pages (4 GiB) | 262,144 pages (2^34 B = 16 GiB) |

The '2^48 bytes' figure that circulates for 64-bit memories is not the core-spec page limit: 2^48 bytes would be only 2^32 pages, i.e. 1/65,536 of the core-spec maximum, and it would sit below the JS API's own declarable field limit of 2^37−1 pages — which is impossible, since an embedding may be stricter than the core spec but never looser. 2^48 is therefore correctly read as the exponent on *pages*, not on bytes, for the core limit.

Version note: these are the WebAssembly 3.0 (memory64-merged) rules. Pre-3.0 documents contain no i64 memory type at all, so the i64 question has no answer there; drafts that predate the memory64 merge also state the 32-bit limit differently in prose while giving the same 65,536-page value.

5. BOUNDARY BEHAVIOUR AT THE LIMIT (for implementers)

- Declaring min = max = 65,536 pages (i32) or min = max = 2^48 pages (i64) is valid.
- Declaring min or max one page above the range k is a validation error; the module is rejected before instantiation.
- min > max is a validation error, independent of k.
- A memory instance's size S satisfies min ≤ S ≤ max (in pages). memory.grow by d succeeds only if S + d ≤ max and the host can allocate; otherwise it returns −1 (i32) and the memory is unchanged. At max = 2^48 pages, S + d is computed on page counts, and the corresponding byte size must be computed in 65-bit-safe arithmetic: 2^48 × 2^16 = 2^64 overflows u64 when expressed as an inclusive byte count (max u64 = 2^64−1), so host code must either keep sizes in pages or use a wider type / explicit saturation check.
- memory.size returns the current size in pages, of the memory's address type (i32 for 32-bit memories, i64 for 64-bit memories); it is a page count, never a byte count.

6. QUICK REFERENCE

  2^16 = 65,536                    (page size in bytes; i32 page cap; also i32 byte cap exponent base)
  2^32 = 4,294,967,296             (i32 byte cap = 4 GiB)
  2^34 = 17,179,869,184            (JS API 64-bit runtime cap in bytes = 16 GiB = 262,144 pages)
  2^37−1 = 137,438,953,471         (JS API 64-bit declarable field cap in pages)
  2^48 = 281,474,976,710,656       (core-spec i64 page cap)
  2^64 = 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 (core-spec i64 byte cap = 16 EiB)

Minimal validation predicate (pseudocode):

  page_size = 65536
  max_pages(at) = 2^16 if at == i32 else 2^48

  valid_limits(at, min_pages, max_pages_opt):
      k = max_pages(at)
      if min_pages > k: return INVALID
      if max_pages_opt is present and (max_pages_opt < min_pages or max_pages_opt > k): return INVALID
      return VALID

  max_bytes(at) = max_pages(at) * page_size   # i32: 2^32; i64: 2^64 (compute in ≥65-bit arithmetic)

# Leakage power-density limits at points >= 5 cm from the external surface

## 1. Answers (all values already in mW/cm2 — no conversion required)

| Part | Jurisdiction / instrument | Condition | Limit at >= 5 cm |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | Canada — Radiation Emitting Devices Regulations, C.R.C., c. 1370, Schedule II, Part III (Microwave Ovens), s. 4(1)(a)(i) | Fully assembled, service and user controls adjusted for maximum output, **prescribed test load in place** | **1.0 mW/cm2** |
| (b) | United States — 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1) | Measured **prior to acquisition by a purchaser** | **1 mW/cm2** |
| (c) | United States — 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1) | **Thereafter** (after acquisition by a purchaser) | **5 mW/cm2** |

Reference conversion only: 1 mW/cm2 = 10 W/m2. Both instruments state their limits directly in milliwatt per square centimetre, so the "give each in mW/cm2" requirement is met without arithmetic.

## 2. Canadian basis — verbatim and parsed

C.R.C., c. 1370, s. 4(1):

> "Every microwave oven shall, when fully assembled and operating with its service controls and user controls adjusted to yield the maximum output, function in such a manner that (a) the leakage radiation, measured with the instrument prescribed by paragraph (3)(b), at all points at least 5 cm from the external surface of the oven, does not exceed (i) 1.0 mW/cm2 with the test load prescribed by paragraph (3)(a) placed ... (ii) 5.0 mW/cm2 without a test load, where the oven is operable in such conditions"

Test load, s. 4(3)(a):
- (i) oven designed for cooking with total microwave power generating capacity **not greater than 1.5 kW**: **275 +/- 15 mL of water at an initial temperature of 20 +/- 5 C**, placed **in the centre of the shelf in the cavity**;
- (ii) any other oven: the substance and amount specified by the manufacturer.

Instrument, s. 4(3)(b):
- capable of measuring a power density of **1.0 mW/cm2 with an accuracy of 2 dB or better**;
- indicator **response time not greater than 3 seconds**.

Co-requisite on the same device (not part of this question, listed so it is not missed at design review): s. 4(1)(b) — X-ray intensity at 5 cm from the external surface shall not exceed **0.5 mR per hour over 10 cm2**.

## 3. United States basis — verbatim and parsed

21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1) — Power density limit:

> "The equivalent plane-wave power density existing in the proximity of the external oven surface shall not exceed 1 milliwatt per square centimeter at any point 5 centimeters or more from the external surface of the oven, measured prior to acquisition by a purchaser, and, thereafter, 5 milliwatts per square centimeter at any such point."

Supporting definitions and conditions:
- 1030.10(b)(7): "external surface" includes doors, door handles, latches and control knobs — the 5 cm envelope is taken from those features, not from the cabinet box alone.
- 1030.10(b)(8): equivalent plane-wave power density = (rms E-field)^2 / 377 ohms.
- 1030.10(c)(3)(i): instrument must reach **90 percent of steady-state reading within 3 seconds** on a step-function input; tests **shall account for all measurement errors and uncertainties** so the power density does not exceed the limit.
- 1030.10(c)(3)(ii): compliance judged on the **maximum reading at the location of greatest emission, through at least one stirrer cycle** (alternative procedures available under 21 CFR 1010.13 for unusual stirrer characteristics).
- 1030.10(c)(3)(iii): oven at **maximum output** with **275 +/- 15 mL of tap water initially at 20 +/- 5 C** at the **centre of the load-carrying surface**.

Note the second appearance of 5 mW/cm2: 1030.10(c)(2)(v) requires the **secondary** interlock to prevent emission above 5 mW/cm2 at >= 5 cm, while the **primary** interlock must hold the 1 mW/cm2 figure. This is a redundancy requirement, not the purchaser limit; it is recorded here so the 5 mW/cm2 number is not mis-attributed.

## 4. Cross-jurisdiction design conclusion

The binding figure for a product shipped to both markets is the **stricter of the pre-acquisition limits**, i.e. **1.0 mW/cm2 at >= 5 cm with the 275 mL water load** — which is identical in both regimes and measured under materially identical load and instrument conditions. The Canadian 1.0 mW/cm2 and the US pre-acquisition 1 mW/cm2 therefore collapse into a single type-test acceptance criterion.

Recommended production/type-test target: **maximum reading <= 0.75 mW/cm2** at any point >= 5 cm, with the water load in place. Rationale: the Canadian instrument tolerance is 2 dB (a factor of 10^(2/10) = 1.26 in power density), and 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(3)(i) requires measurement uncertainty to be accounted for such that the true value does not exceed 1 mW/cm2. 0.75 x 1.26 = 0.944 mW/cm2, which stays under 1.0. Designing to the 5 mW/cm2 post-acquisition figure is a compliance error: that figure is an in-service/service-adjustment ceiling, not a manufacturing limit.

## 5. Single test procedure that discharges both jurisdictions

1. Assemble the oven fully; set service and user controls to yield maximum output.
2. Load: 275 +/- 15 mL of tap water at 20 +/- 5 C, vessel at the centre of the load-carrying surface / centre of the shelf. (Canada and US load specifications coincide for ovens <= 1.5 kW.)
3. Survey probe: meter meeting both instrument clauses — accuracy 2 dB or better and 90 % of steady state within 3 s (a <= 3 s indicator response satisfies both).
4. Scan all external surfaces at **>= 5 cm**, including door, door handle, latch, control knobs and seams; hold each location through **at least one complete stirrer cycle**; record the maximum reading.
5. Compare max reading **plus measurement uncertainty** against **1.0 mW/cm2**. This single result demonstrates (a) and (b).
6. Optional/extra Canadian point: repeat with **no test load**, if the oven is operable in that condition, and compare against **5.0 mW/cm2** (s. 4(1)(a)(ii)).
7. Post-market/service check (US (c) only): the same survey after acquisition is judged against **5 mW/cm2**; this is the figure a service technician or purchaser-side verifier applies.

## 6. Points of confusion to avoid

- Canada's 5.0 mW/cm2 is a **no-load** condition limit (s. 4(1)(a)(ii)); the US 5 mW/cm2 is a **post-acquisition** limit (1030.10(c)(1)). They are numerically equal and legally unrelated — do not cite one as the other.
- Both regimes say "at any point 5 cm **or more**", so exactly 5.0 cm is inside the envelope and every point further out is too; a reading taken closer than 5 cm is not comparable to either limit.
- "Domestic" does not create a separate limit tier in either regime. The only classification split in the Canadian text is by **total microwave power generating capacity (<= 1.5 kW vs > 1.5 kW)**, which changes the prescribed load, not the 1.0 mW/cm2 number. The interlock-cycle requirement (s. 4(6)) splits commercial vs other ovens (200 000 vs 100 000 cycles) — again not a leakage-limit tier.

## 7. Versions relied on

- Canada: Radiation Emitting Devices Regulations, C.R.C., c. 1370, consolidation current to 2026-10-29, last amended 2025-10-09 (Justice Laws full text).
- United States: 21 CFR 1030.10, eCFR current text; corroborated against CFR 2025 edition, Title 21, Volume 8, page 944.

Scope note: state-level US requirements and any Canadian provincial requirements were not assessed; they are outside the two federal instruments named in the request and do not change the figures above.

question: X32
shape: Occupational noise, Great Britain statutory instrument
answer:
ADVISORY NOTE — LEGAL NOISE EXPOSURE LIMIT VALUES AND THE STATUS OF HEARING PROTECTOR ATTENUATION
Applicable law: Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 (SI 2005/1643), regulation 4, as they apply in Great Britain (E+W+S).

=====================================================================
1. THE VALUES (regulation 4)
=====================================================================
Regulation 4 sets three tiers of value, each in two currencies: daily or weekly personal noise exposure (A-weighted, LEP,d / LEP,w) and peak sound pressure (C-weighted). The full set is reproduced below because the limit values cannot be used correctly in isolation from the action values.

| Tier | Daily or weekly personal noise exposure | Peak sound pressure | Protector attenuation counted? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lower exposure action value — reg 4(1) | 80 dB(A) | 135 dB(C) | NO |
| Upper exposure action value — reg 4(2) | 85 dB(A) | 137 dB(C) | NO |
| **Exposure limit value — reg 4(3)** | **87 dB(A)** | **140 dB(C)** | **YES** |

ANSWER TO ASK 1 — the legal exposure limit values are:
  (a) a daily or weekly personal noise exposure of 87 dB(A); and
  (b) a peak sound pressure of 140 dB(C).

Statutory wording (reg 4(3)): 'The exposure limit values are — (a) a daily or weekly personal noise exposure of 87 dB (A-weighted); and (b) a peak sound pressure of 140 dB (C-weighted).'

An 'exposure limit value' is defined in reg 2 as 'the level of daily or weekly personal noise exposure or of peak sound pressure set out in regulation 4 which must not be exceeded'. It is a prohibition, not a target. It sits above, and does not displace, the general duty in reg 6(1) to eliminate or reduce exposure to as low a level as is reasonably practicable — compliance with 87 dB(A) is not by itself compliance with the Regulations.

=====================================================================
2. WHETHER PROTECTOR ATTENUATION MAY BE COUNTED AT THE UPPER EXPOSURE ACTION VALUE
=====================================================================
ANSWER TO ASK 2 — NO. Hearing protector attenuation may not be counted when judging whether the upper exposure action value has been reached (nor the lower exposure action value).

Statutory basis, reg 4(5), verbatim: 'In applying the exposure limit values in paragraph (3), but not in applying the lower and upper exposure action values in paragraphs (1) and (2), account shall be taken of the protection given to the employee by any personal hearing protectors provided by the employer in accordance with regulation 7(2).'

So the position is a deliberate asymmetry:

  • Exposure action values (80/85 dB(A); 135/137 dB(C)) are judged on the noise exposure at the employee's ear BEFORE any allowance for hearing protection. If the unattenuated exposure reaches or exceeds 85 dB(A) or 137 dB(C), the upper exposure action value has been reached and the duties it triggers apply in full, even if issued protectors nominally reduce the exposure below 85 dB(A).
  • Exposure limit values (87 dB(A); 140 dB(C)) are judged AT THE EAR, i.e. WITH the attenuation of protectors provided under reg 7(2) taken into account. This is why the limit value is set at 87 dB(A) rather than at a level that would be tolerable unprotected.

Consequences that follow directly from this, and which are commonly got wrong:

  1. A noise assessment that applies an SNR/HML/octave-band deduction before comparing the result with 85 dB(A) is wrong in law. The comparison with 80 and 85 dB(A) (and with 135 and 137 dB(C)) must be made on the measured/estimated exposure without protection.
  2. The reg 6(2) programme of measures (elimination/reduction by means other than hearing protection, to as low a level as reasonably practicable) is triggered by the unattenuated exposure reaching 85 dB(A) or 137 dB(C). Fitting protectors does not switch that duty off. The Explanatory Memorandum to the Regulations is explicit that this is 'a programme of measures, excluding the provision of personal hearing protectors'.
  3. Reg 7(2) requires the employer, if unable by other means to reduce exposure below the upper exposure action value, to provide personal hearing protectors to any employee so exposed. The trigger is again the unattenuated exposure.
  4. Reg 7(3) Hearing Protection Zone designation, demarcation, access restriction and the 'no entry unless wearing protectors' duty are triggered where an employee is likely to be exposed at or above the upper exposure action value — again judged without attenuation.
  5. Health surveillance duties (reg 9) attach to employees at risk where exposure is at or above the upper exposure action value, judged without attenuation.
  6. The exposure limit value is the one place where attenuation is counted — and then only the protection given by protectors 'provided by the employer in accordance with regulation 7(2)'. Two practical points flow from that wording: (i) the calculation must reflect the protection actually achievable in the workplace, not the laboratory rating on the packet; (ii) protectors merely made available on request under reg 7(1) arguably fall outside the reg 4(5) wording, so an employer who is above the upper action value should be providing protectors under reg 7(2) as well as making them available under reg 7(1).

=====================================================================
3. HOW THE ATTENUATION IS COUNTED AT THE EXPOSURE LIMIT VALUE (method, not law)
=====================================================================
The Regulations fix the values; they do not prescribe the calculation. Standard practice (HSE guidance L108; BS EN 458; ISO 4869-2) is:
  • Octave-band method — most accurate; compare octave-band levels of the noise with the protector's octave-band mean attenuation plus standard deviation.
  • HML method — where M (medium) and H (high) values and L (low) are available; select the formula by the C-weighted minus A-weighted level difference.
  • SNR method — single-number rating, least precise: estimated level at the ear ≈ LEX (unattenuated) − (SNR − derating).
Real-world protection is routinely poorer than the laboratory rating because of fitting, wear time and condition. A common conservative convention is to deduct the SNR minus a margin (HSE historically suggested assuming protection of SNR − 5 dB or similar, and BS EN 458 gives a derating scheme by protector class).
Arithmetic illustration only (not a compliance conclusion): 93 dB(A) unattenuated, SNR 25 derated to 20 dB, gives approximately 73 dB(A) at the ear — within the 87 dB(A) limit value, while the same 93 dB(A) remains above the 85 dB(A) upper exposure action value for the purpose of regs 6(2), 7(2), 7(3) and 9.

=====================================================================
4. DAILY VERSUS WEEKLY AVERAGING
=====================================================================
Reg 4(4): where an employee's exposure varies markedly from day to day, the employer may use weekly personal noise exposure in place of daily personal noise exposure for the purpose of compliance with the Regulations. Weekly averaging is a permitted substitution, not a general option, and it does not permit any day's peak to be averaged away — the 140 dB(C) limit value applies to the peak, full stop. Exposure is ascertained in accordance with Schedule 1 (daily, Part 1; weekly, Part 2) and peak sound pressure in accordance with Schedule 2.

=====================================================================
5. COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST FOR THE EMPLOYER
=====================================================================
  1. Measure/estimate personal exposure and peak at the ear with NO allowance for protectors.
  2. Compare against 80/135 and 85/137. Record which action values are reached or exceeded on that basis.
  3. Where 85 dB(A) or 137 dB(C) is reached: implement the reg 6(2) programme (not hearing protection), provide protectors under reg 7(2), designate and demarcate Hearing Protection Zones under reg 7(3), and provide health surveillance under reg 9.
  4. Separately, calculate exposure at the ear WITH the attenuation of the protectors actually provided and worn, using a defensible method and a realistic derating, and compare against 87 dB(A) / 140 dB(C). If that comparison shows the limit value reached or exceeded, treat it as a breach requiring immediate action, investigation of the cause, and amendment of the control measures.
  5. Do not use the step-4 result to justify not doing step 3.

=====================================================================
6. ASSUMPTIONS, SCOPE AND CAVEATS
=====================================================================
  • Jurisdiction: Great Britain. Northern Ireland has parallel provision in the Control of Noise at Work Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2006 (SR 2006/1) with the same values; outside GB, verify the local instrument.
  • Sector: the general manufacturing/industrial regime. The music and entertainment sector has its own defined terms and history within the 2005 Regulations; special categories (e.g. seafarers, offshore) may have separate or additional provision. Confirm before relying on this note for those workforces.
  • The values quoted are those of reg 4 as amended and in force; they are unchanged across the versions consulted (as made, 2015, 2020 point-in-time).
  • The description of regs 6, 7 and 9 in section 2 is a paraphrase for orientation; the operative words for ask 2 are those of reg 4(5), quoted verbatim above, and those for ask 1 are those of reg 4(3), also quoted verbatim.
  • This note addresses the legal values and the counting rule only. It does not constitute the noise risk assessment required by reg 5, nor advice on protector selection for a specific noise spectrum.

- R_infinity (2018) = 10973731.568160 m^-1, u = 0.000021 m^-1

The 2018 uncertainty is included because the request asks "what was the CODATA 2018 value it replaced" and a like-for-like comparison of a measured constant is only meaningful with its uncertainty; the central value alone is the direct answer to ask 3, and the uncertainty is supplied as supporting context, not as a separate claim.

## 2. Sources (primary NIST pages only)

1. **CODATA 2022, value page (asks 1 and 2).** NIST CODATA Value: Rydberg constant, https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?ryd — page footer states "Source: 2022 CODATA recommended values". Page text, verbatim fields: "Numerical value 10 973 731.568 157 m-1"; "Standard uncertainty 0.000 012 m-1"; "Relative standard uncertainty 1.1 x 10-12"; "Concise form 10 973 731.568 157(12) m-1".
2. **CODATA 2022, wall chart (independent confirmation of asks 1 and 2).** "CODATA RECOMMENDED VALUES OF THE FUNDAMENTAL PHYSICAL CONSTANTS: 2022", NIST SP 961 (May 2024), https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/pdf/wall_2022.pdf — line reads "Rydberg constant R_inf 10 973 731.568 157(12) [m-1]". Retrieved 2026-11-18T01:07:10Z (sha256 5b7f6d0a2dd9).
3. **CODATA 2018, extensive listing (ask 3).** "2018 CODATA adjustment", Fundamental Physical Constants — Extensive Listing, https://physics.nist.gov/cuu//pdf/all_2018.pdf — line reads "Rydberg constant R_inf 10 973 731.568 160(21) [m-1] 1.9 x 10-12". Retrieved 2026-11-18T01:07:11Z (sha256 0baec5980ef4).
4. **CODATA 2018, wallet card (cross-check of ask 3).** "2018 CODATA RECOMMENDED VALUES OF THE FUNDAMENTAL CONSTANTS OF PHYSICS AND CHEMISTRY", NIST SP 959 (June 2019), wallet_2018.pdf — lists the same 2018 adjustment; its Rydberg frequency line "3.289 841 960 2508(64) x 10^15 Hz" is the 2018 cR_inf entry corresponding to the 2018 R_inf above, and differs from the 2022 cR_inf entry "3.289 841 960 2500(36) x 10^15 Hz", confirming that the two revisions are being kept distinct.

## 3. Conventions used (and why)

- **Uncertainty representation.** NIST's own footnote, quoted from the 2022 wall chart: "a number in parentheses, if present, is the one-standard-deviation uncertainty in the last two digits." Both the numeric form and the parenthetical form are given above; they are the same number. 157(12) means 10 973 731.568 157 +/- 0.000 000 000 012 — i.e. the parenthetical 12 sits in the last two digits of the quoted decimals, which here are the 10^-6 place and the 10^-7 place, giving 0.000 012 m^-1.
- **Uncertainty is k = 1** (one standard deviation), as published. It is not an expanded uncertainty at 95 % coverage and must not be multiplied by a coverage factor of 2 unless a 95 % interval is explicitly wanted.
- **No unit conversion.** The published unit is m^-1 (NIST's full description: "cycles or periods per meter"), so the figures are quoted as published. No wavenumber-to-energy or wavenumber-to-wavelength conversion has been applied.
- **Precision.** All digits as published by NIST are retained; nothing has been rounded or truncated. The 2022 and 2018 values happen to be quoted to the same number of decimal places (6 decimals, 10^-6 m^-1 resolution), so they can be compared digit-for-digit.
- **Symbol.** R_infinity (R with subscript infinity) is the Rydberg constant, the limit for infinite nuclear mass. It is a different constant from the Rydberg constants for specific systems (e.g. R_H for hydrogen), which carry different numerical values; those are not reported here and should not be substituted.

## 4. Verification arithmetic

1. Parenthetical-to-numeric check, 2022: 157(12) -> u = 0.000 012 m^-1. This equals the separately published "Standard uncertainty 0.000 012 m-1" on the CUU value page. Consistent.
2. Relative-uncertainty check, 2022: 0.000 012 / 10 973 731.568 157 = 1.09 x 10^-12, which rounds to the published 1.1 x 10^-12. Consistent.
3. Parenthetical-to-numeric check, 2018: 160(21) -> u = 0.000 021 m^-1. Relative check: 0.000 021 / 10 973 731.568 160 = 1.91 x 10^-12, which rounds to the published 1.9 x 10^-12. Consistent.

This shift is 0.14 times the 2018 standard uncertainty (0.000 021 m^-1) and 0.25 times the 2022 standard uncertainty (0.000 012 m^-1), so the two recommended values are mutually consistent at well under one standard deviation. The change is a normal outcome of a re-adjustment, not a discrepancy, and no significance should be attached to the direction of the shift.
5. Uncertainty ratio: 0.000 021 / 0.000 012 = 1.75, so the 2022 uncertainty is smaller by a factor of about 1.75. No other reduction factor is claimed.
6. Digit-integrity check: the integer part 10 973 731 is identical in both adjustments (seven digits before the decimal point plus the 10^7 scale); only the decimals differ, in the third decimal place. This is the check that guards against the most common transcription error in this constant.

## 5. Audit note

If this answer is re-used or quoted later, quote the revision label along with the number ("CODATA 2022" vs. "CODATA 2018") and, where the value matters to more than the 10^-6 m^-1 level, quote the parenthetical form exactly as published. TRAFFIC ENGINEERING MEMO — MUTCD PEDESTRIAN INTERVAL PROVISIONS (11th Ed., Dec. 2023, §4I.06 vs. 2009 Ed., §4E.06)

ANSWERS AT A GLANCE
| # | Question | Answer | Status of requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Minimum buffer interval (steady UPRAISED HAND) after the pedestrian change interval, before release of a conflicting vehicular movement — MUTCD 11th Ed. §4I.06 | 2 seconds | Standard (shall) — mandatory |
| 2 | Default walking speed for sizing pedestrian clearance time — MUTCD 11th Ed. §4I.06 | 3.5 ft/s | Guidance (should); 2.8 ft/s is a conditional alternative, not the default |
| 3 | Buffer-interval minimum in the 2009 MUTCD (§4E.06) | 3 seconds | Standard (shall) — mandatory |

Net change 2009 -> 11th Ed.: buffer minimum reduced from 3 s to 2 s; default walking speed reduced from 4 ft/s to 3.5 ft/s (with the older/disabled-pedestrian consideration moving from 3 ft/s to 2.8 ft/s).

=====================================================================
1. MINIMUM BUFFER INTERVAL — 2 SECONDS (11th EDITION, §4I.06)
=====================================================================
Governing text (Standard, §4I.06 ¶04), as reproduced in the California MUTCD 2026 Edition final draft — '(FHWA's MUTCD 2023 Edition, as amended for use in California)', Chapter 4I, page 1272:

  'A pedestrian change interval consisting of a flashing UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall begin immediately following the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication except as provided in Section 4F.19. Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement. The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time (see Paragraphs 7 through 16 of this Section). The buffer interval shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used.'

Corroborated independently by Figure 4I-4 'Pedestrian Intervals', which labels the buffer interval '2 seconds MIN.' and adds the note: 'The Buffer Interval, which shall always be provided and displayed, may be used to help satisfy the calculated pedestrian clearance time, or may begin after the calculated pedestrian clearance time has ended.'

Engineering reading — four binding points for a timing plan:
(a) 2.0 s is a floor, not a target. It is expressed as 'at least', so 2.0 s is the minimum acceptable value; a value of 1.9 s is non-compliant.
(b) The buffer is always required ('shall always be provided and displayed'). There is no case in the 11th Edition where a pedestrian phase may release conflicting traffic with zero buffer.
(c) The buffer may be counted toward the calculated pedestrian clearance time (change interval + buffer >= pedestrian clearance time). This is a change in accounting, not a waiver of the 2 s floor — a 2 s buffer still has to physically exist.
(d) Placement: the buffer may not begin later than the start of the red clearance interval, if one is used. During the yellow change interval the UPRAISED HAND may be flashing, steady, or flashing then steady (Option, ¶05), so a buffer that coincides with the yellow change interval satisfies the 2 s requirement provided the yellow is at least 3 s — which it must be independently.
(e) Display detail: the countdown numerals terminate with the pedestrian change interval; during the buffer the steady UPRAISED HAND remains displayed while the countdown display goes dark ('After the countdown displays zero, the display shall remain dark until the beginning of the next countdown').

Provenance note: the verbatim text above is from the California MUTCD 2026 draft reproducing the FHWA 2023 Edition. The paragraph carries no California amendment marking and reads as base Standard text, so 2 s is taken as the FHWA 11th Edition value. One-line verification if a stamped copy is required: open the FHWA MUTCD 11th Edition Part 4 PDF, Chapter 4I, Section 4I.06, paragraph 04, and confirm 'at least 2 seconds' and the '2 seconds MIN.' label in Figure 4I-4.

=====================================================================
2. DEFAULT WALKING SPEED FOR PEDESTRIAN CLEARANCE TIME — 3.5 FT/S
=====================================================================
§4I.06 (Guidance, ¶¶9–10a in the reproduced numbering) sets the baseline and then two conditional reductions:

  Baseline/default: pedestrian clearance time is sized on a walking speed of 3.5 feet per second (3.5 ft/s = 1.07 m/s).
  Conditional: '...a walking speed of less than 3.5 feet per second should be considered in determining the pedestrian clearance time' where pedestrians who walk slower than 3.5 ft/s, or pedestrians who use wheelchairs, routinely use the crosswalk.
  Conditional: '10a Where older or disabled pedestrians routinely use the crosswalk, a walking speed of 2.8 feet per second should be considered in determining the pedestrian clearance time.' (2.8 ft/s = 0.85 m/s)

So the default for sizing is 3.5 ft/s. The 2.8 ft/s value is an explicit, site-conditional lower speed triggered by routine use of the crosswalk by older or disabled pedestrians; it is not the default and must not be applied blanket-wide, nor may the default 3.5 ft/s be used at a site where that condition plainly exists without documenting the engineering judgment.

Worked check (60 ft, curb to far curb of the traveled way):
  Pedestrian clearance time = 60 ft / 3.5 ft/s = 17.14 s.
  Select 16 s pedestrian change interval (flashing UPRAISED HAND) + 2 s buffer = 18 s >= 17.14 s — satisfies both the sum rule and the 2 s buffer minimum.
  Same crossing at 2.8 ft/s (older/disabled condition): 60 / 2.8 = 21.43 s -> 20 s change interval + 2 s buffer = 22 s >= 21.43 s.
Note the interaction with ¶07 Guidance for a pedestrian signal head with no concurrent vehicular phase: the flashing UPRAISED HAND 'should be set to be approximately 4 seconds less than the required pedestrian clearance time' with the steady UPRAISED HAND making up the balance before the conflicting vehicular phase starts. A plan that satisfies the sum rule but leaves the buffer at 2 s must still respect that 4-second relationship where the no-concurrent-phase condition applies.

=====================================================================
3. BUFFER-INTERVAL MINIMUM IN THE 2009 MUTCD — 3 SECONDS
=====================================================================
2009 MUTCD, Section 4E.06 'Pedestrian Intervals and Signal Phases', paragraph 5 (Standard), required a buffer interval of steady UPRAISED HAND 'for at least 3 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement', with the same accompanying provisions that the sum of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time and that the buffer not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used. The 2009 edition's pedestrian interval figure likewise carried the 3-second buffer minimum.

Change summary 2009 -> 11th Edition:
  Buffer interval minimum: 3 s -> 2 s (reduced by 1 s).
  Default walking speed: 4 ft/s -> 3.5 ft/s (context; not one of the three asks).
  Older/disabled-pedestrian walking speed: 3 ft/s -> 2.8 ft/s (context).
  Buffer now explicitly always provided and explicitly countable toward the calculated pedestrian clearance time.
Practical consequence: the 11th Edition cuts the fixed buffer by 1 s but slows the design walking speed by 0.5 ft/s, which lengthens the calculated clearance time roughly 14 percent on a given crossing. Because the buffer may now be counted inside the clearance time, a retimed plan generally keeps the same overall pedestrian phase length while shifting roughly a second out of the flashing DON'T WALK and into the steady buffer — the total pedestrian time does not automatically grow by the full clearance-time increase.

Provenance note: the 2009 figure above is stated from the 2009 MUTCD text (§4E.06 ¶5); the 2009 Part 4 PDF was among the sources consulted but no 2009 passage was reproduced in the extracted excerpts, unlike the 11th Edition text. Verification is a single lookup: 2009 MUTCD Part 4, Section 4E.06, paragraph 5, confirm 'at least 3 seconds'. If a locally adopted edition or a state supplement governs, check that document instead — several state manuals retained the 3-second buffer after the 11th Edition was published.

=====================================================================
4. CONFIDENCE AND VERIFICATION TABLE
=====================================================================
| Item | Value | Basis | Confidence | Verification step |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 11th Ed. buffer minimum | 2 s | Quoted Standard text + Figure 4I-4 label | High | FHWA 11th Ed. Part 4, §4I.06 ¶04 |
| 11th Ed. default walking speed | 3.5 ft/s | Quoted Guidance text | High | FHWA 11th Ed. Part 4, §4I.06 ¶¶9–10a |
| 11th Ed. conditional walking speed | 2.8 ft/s | Quoted Guidance text | High | Same |
| 2009 buffer minimum | 3 s | Engineer's knowledge of §4E.06 ¶5 | Medium-high | 2009 MUTCD Part 4, §4E.06 ¶5 |
| 2009 walking speeds (context) | 4 ft/s default / 3 ft/s older-disabled | Engineer's knowledge of §4E.06 | Medium | Same |

Two caveats a reviewer should carry forward: (i) paragraph numbers differ between the FHWA 11th Edition and state reproductions (the California draft inserts a '10a'), so cite by section and by the quoted sentence rather than by paragraph number alone when writing a legal description; (ii) MUTCD applicability is by adoption date and by state supplement — the 2 s / 3.5 ft/s answers bind only where the 11th Edition has been adopted.

# Thermal data for ATmega328P, 28-pin PDIP, in Microchip DS40002061B (09/2020)

## 1. Finding

Both halves of the question come back negative against this document, and the negative is the deliverable:

- **Junction-to-ambient thermal resistance (degC/W): not specified.** DS40002061B publishes no theta_JA value for the ATmega328P in the 28-pin PDIP (Microchip package code **28P3**, 28-lead, 0.300 in wide PDIP), and no theta_JA for any other package in the family either. There is no thermal-resistance table, no thermal-characteristics section, and no theta_JA/theta_JC row in Absolute Maximum Ratings or DC Characteristics.
- **Maximum junction temperature or total power dissipation: not specified.** The document gives no T_J(max) and no P_tot rating. What it gives instead are absolute-maximum **current** limits and an **ambient** temperature range (Section 2 below). Those are frequently mistaken for a power rating; they are not one.

A degC/W number or a wattage attributed to this datasheet would be fabricated. Anyone quoting, say, "about 50-60 degC/W for PDIP" is quoting a package-level figure from a different Microchip document (or from memory), not this datasheet.

## 2. What DS40002061B does specify (the nearest neighbours, and why they are not the answer)

| Item | Value | Where | Why it is not the answer to ask 1 or 2 |

| DC current, VCC and GND pins | 200.0 mA | Absolute Maximum Ratings | Sum of supply-pin currents, not dissipated power; no voltage term, so no watts |

Consequence for design: because there is no P_tot and no T_J(max), you cannot close a junction-temperature calculation from this datasheet alone. The 40 mA/pin and 200 mA supply-pin figures are current budgets for pin and bond-wire integrity, and they are routinely the binding constraint long before self-heating is; the port-group sums (150 mA sourcing / 100 mA sinking) are the ones that actually bite, because they are spent by pins that are each individually well inside their own limit.

## 3. Where the thermal number actually lives

Package thermal resistance for 28P3 is a **package** property published outside the device datasheet:

1. Microchip's package thermal data documentation (theta_JA / theta_JC / theta_JB tables keyed by package code such as 28P3), and the package outline drawing for 28P3 in the datasheet's Packaging Information section (dimensions only - do not expect theta_JA there).
2. Microchip's product page for ATmega328P under Documentation / Design Resources, which links the package thermal data separately from DS40002061B.
3. If no vendor figure is obtainable: JEDEC JESD51-2 / JESD51-3 / JESD51-7 board-conditional characterisation, or measure. theta_JA is meaningless without stating the test board; a 28P3 figure on a JESD51-3 low-effective-conductivity board and on a JESD51-7 high-effective-conductivity board differ substantially.

## 5. Calculation template (illustrative only - the theta_JA placeholder is NOT a datasheet value)

Once theta_JA for 28P3 is in hand:

    T_J = T_A + P_diss * theta_JA
    P_diss ~= V_CC * I_CC(total) + sum over I/O pins of (V_OL or (V_CC - V_OH)) * I_OL/OH

Check at the worst-case ambient of the ordering code in use (-40 degC to +85 degC industrial) and require T_J <= T_J(max), where T_J(max) must come from a Microchip absolute-maximum statement (commonly the 125 degC operating-temperature ceiling) - it is **not** published in DS40002061B as a junction limit and must be sourced and cited separately.

Worked shape of the arithmetic, with a deliberately blank theta_JA so nothing here can be mistaken for a datasheet figure: at T_A = 85 degC and P_diss = 0.25 W, each 10 degC/W of theta_JA adds 2.5 degC of junction rise. That sensitivity, not a specific number, is the design-relevant statement this datasheet supports.

Note the pin-level asymmetry the datasheet does quantify: an I/O pin is only guaranteed to 4.2 V while sourcing 20 mA and 0.9 V while sinking 20 mA at 5 V, 85 degC. Read as series resistance that is 40 ohm sourcing and 45 ohm sinking - a real dissipation term that does not appear on the schematic and must be included in P_diss when driving LEDs or other loads.
